items.title: 1. Brain and spinal cord perfusion: the physiology behind neurocritical care
items.body:
## 1.1 Why the brain is uniquely vulnerable

- The adult brain accounts for roughly 2% of body weight yet receives approximately 15% of cardiac output and consumes about 20% of resting oxygen.
- Normal average cerebral blood flow (CBF) is approximately 45–55 mL/100 g/min, with regional variation: cortical grey matter has substantially greater flow than white matter.
- Cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO₂) is approximately 3–3.5 mL O₂/100 g/min.
- Neurons contain little energy reserve; interruption of oxidative phosphorylation rapidly impairs Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase, producing membrane depolarisation, cytotoxic oedema, calcium influx, excitotoxic glutamate release, mitochondrial injury and eventually irreversible cell death.
- The threshold is not a single universal CBF value: duration, temperature, metabolic demand and collateral circulation all matter.

- When cerebral flow falls modestly, oxygen extraction increases and electrical activity may fail before cellular integrity is lost.
- The **ischaemic penumbra** is therefore dysfunctional but potentially salvageable tissue surrounding an irreversibly infarcted core.
- This principle explains why rapid revascularisation is so effective in selected ischaemic strokes and why hypotension, fever, hypoxaemia and seizures can enlarge otherwise survivable injury.

## 1.2 Intracranial compartments and the Monro–Kellie doctrine

- In the adult, the rigid cranial vault contains approximately 80% brain tissue, 10% blood and 10% cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), although proportions vary.
- Since the total volume is approximately fixed, adding a mass, oedema or blood initially displaces venous blood and CSF into the spinal compartment.
- During this **compensated** phase intracranial pressure (ICP) rises relatively little.
- Once compliance is exhausted, small additional volumes cause a steep pressure rise.
- Thus the pressure–volume curve is nonlinear, and an expanding subdural haematoma can change from apparently stable to catastrophic deterioration over minutes.

- Normal adult supine ICP is often around 5–15 mmHg; interpretation depends on posture, ventilation, age and clinical setting.
- Sustained ICP elevation compromises CPP, compresses veins, increases oedema and may force brain tissue across fixed dural boundaries.
- The classic herniation syndromes are subfalcine (cingulate; anterior cerebral artery compression), uncal/transtentorial (ipsilateral third-nerve dysfunction with a dilating pupil, reduced consciousness, possible posterior cerebral artery infarction), central downward herniation, and tonsillar herniation (brainstem respiratory/circulatory failure).
- A unilateral blown pupil is an emergency, not a finding to await routine repeat imaging.

**Cerebral perfusion pressure:**

- CPP = MAP (at cerebral arterial level) − ICP.
- When central venous pressure exceeds ICP, venous pressure may become the effective downstream pressure, so the simplistic formula can mislead.
- A MAP of 85 mmHg and an ICP of 25 mmHg implies CPP ≈60 mmHg; reducing MAP to 65 mmHg while leaving ICP unchanged drops CPP to ≈40 mmHg. When head-up, the pressure transducer zero level matters: measuring MAP at the heart rather than at the external auditory meatus overestimates the perfusion pressure at the brain.

## 1.3 Cerebral autoregulation, carbon dioxide, oxygen and metabolic coupling

- Normal cerebral arterioles constrict when perfusion pressure rises and dilate when it falls, maintaining relatively stable flow across a broad MAP range.
- The often-taught 50–150 mmHg autoregulatory limits are illustrative population approximations, **not** fixed individual thresholds.
- Chronic hypertension may shift the curve rightward.
- Ischaemia, contusion, sepsis, severe TBI and volatile anaesthesia can impair autoregulation, leaving CBF pressure-passive: then even brief hypotension is dangerous, whereas severe hypertension can exacerbate oedema or bleeding.

- CO₂ is a potent physiological regulator of cerebral vascular tone.
- Within the usual clinical range, CBF changes approximately 2–4% per 1 mmHg change in PaCO₂, but the relationship is nonlinear and depends on baseline CO₂, injury and anaesthetic agents.
- Hypercapnia increases cerebral blood volume and ICP; hypocapnia produces vasoconstriction and reduces ICP but may worsen tissue ischaemia.
- Therefore controlled ventilation usually aims for normocapnia (PaCO₂ ≈35–45 mmHg), and brief moderate hyperventilation is a temporising measure during imminent herniation, not a maintenance strategy.
- Severe prophylactic hyperventilation (PaCO₂ ≤25 mmHg) is discouraged in TBI.

- Arterial oxygen tension has relatively little effect on CBF until marked hypoxaemia, at which point vasodilatation attempts to preserve delivery.
- The aim is to prevent hypoxaemia without assuming supranormal PaO₂ is beneficial.

Anaesthetic drugs modify CMRO₂ and CBF:

- Propofol generally reduces metabolic demand and CBF while preserving flow–metabolism coupling.
- Volatile agents reduce CMRO₂ but cause dose-dependent cerebral vasodilatation.
- Ketamine is no longer considered absolutely contraindicated in brain injury when ventilation and haemodynamics are controlled.

- Fever and seizures markedly increase cerebral metabolic demand.
- Hypothermia lowers CMRO₂ but routine prophylactic therapeutic hypothermia has not shown a reliable neurological outcome benefit in severe TBI and has risks.

## 1.4 Cerebrospinal fluid, cerebral venous drainage and intracranial pressure

- CSF is mainly produced by the choroid plexuses, with a normal adult production rate around 0.3–0.4 mL/min (roughly 500 mL/day).
- It flows through the lateral ventricles, foramina of Monro, third ventricle, aqueduct, fourth ventricle and subarachnoid space, and is absorbed through arachnoid granulations and other pathways.
- Aqueduct obstruction causes noncommunicating hydrocephalus; impaired CSF resorption after blood enters the subarachnoid space may cause communicating hydrocephalus.
- An external ventricular drain (EVD) can both monitor pressure and remove CSF, unlike an intraparenchymal transducer.

- Venous outflow depends on unobstructed jugular drainage and adequate intrathoracic conditions.
- Neck flexion/rotation, tight collars or tracheostomy ties, coughing, agitation, high PEEP when it compromises venous drainage, and marked intra-abdominal pressure can all worsen ICP.
- Head elevation at approximately 30° with the neck midline is helpful if it does not lower arterial pressure at the brain; correct hypotension rather than accepting an attractive ICP number with inadequate CPP.

## 1.5 Blood supply of the brain: anatomy predicts clinical syndrome

- The internal carotid arteries supply the anterior circulation through the anterior cerebral (ACA) and middle cerebral (MCA) arteries; the vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery supplying the posterior circulation and posterior cerebral arteries (PCAs).
- The Circle of Willis provides potential collateral channels via anterior and posterior communicating arteries, but completeness and functional adequacy vary.
- An MCA occlusion commonly causes contralateral face/arm weakness and sensory deficit, aphasia (dominant hemisphere), neglect (nondominant hemisphere), and gaze preference toward the lesion.
- ACA territory infarction may predominantly affect the leg with abulia
- PCA infarction causes contralateral homonymous visual field loss
- Vertebrobasilar ischaemia causes diplopia, vertigo, ataxia, dysarthria, dysphagia, crossed brainstem signs or profound consciousness impairment.
- **A low NIHSS does not exclude a dangerous posterior-circulation stroke.**

- The anterior choroidal and lenticulostriate arteries are end-arteries with poor collateral capacity, making deep structures vulnerable to occlusion and hypertensive haemorrhage.
- Cerebellar infarction may swell in the confined posterior fossa, obstruct the fourth ventricle and compress the brainstem; early neurosurgical decompression or ventricular drainage may be lifesaving.
- A posterior communicating artery aneurysm can compress the third cranial nerve, producing painful ptosis, eye deviation and pupil dilation; investigate urgently even before rupture.

## 1.6 Spinal cord vascular anatomy and spinal cord perfusion

- The **single anterior spinal artery** perfuses the anterior two-thirds of the cord, including corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts; paired posterior spinal arteries perfuse dorsal columns.
- Radiculomedullary contributors enter segmentally, with a variable dominant lower thoracolumbar supply (artery of Adamkiewicz, commonly left-sided around T8–L1).
- The mid-thoracic cord is particularly vulnerable because collateral supply is limited.
- Spinal cord perfusion pressure (SCPP) can be approximated as MAP minus the larger of CSF pressure and local venous pressure.
- This is why hypotension, high CSF pressure and reduced segmental arterial flow may interact during thoracic aortic surgery, acute cord trauma or epidural haematoma.

- Anterior cord syndrome causes bilateral motor weakness and loss of pain/temperature below the lesion with relative preservation of dorsal-column vibration/proprioception.
- Posterior cord injury does the opposite.
- A hemicord injury (Brown–Séquard syndrome) causes ipsilateral weakness/proprioceptive loss and contralateral pain-temperature loss beginning several segments below.
- Distinguish a **spinal cord syndrome** from isolated cauda equina lesions, which cause lower motor neuron weakness, radicular pain and saddle or sphincter dysfunction.
- A new spinal deficit after neuraxial blockade requires urgent exclusion of compression and is not safely attributed to residual local anaesthetic.

items.body:
## 2.1 Coma is a syndrome, not a diagnosis

- Consciousness requires an intact bilateral cerebral hemispheric network and ascending arousal pathways through the brainstem and thalamus.
- A patient may become comatose because of diffuse physiological/metabolic suppression (hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, hypercapnia, toxic drugs, hepatic failure), bilateral hemispheric injury (diffuse hypoxic ischaemia, extensive oedema, bilateral infarction) or brainstem pathology (basilar occlusion, haemorrhage, compression).
- Unilateral lesions usually cause coma only when mass effect disturbs the opposite hemisphere or diencephalic/brainstem structures.

- The immediate task is to **stabilise and search for reversible causes in parallel**.
- Treat airway compromise with manual airway management, suction and intubation when required to protect against aspiration or prevent secondary brain injury.
- Secure oxygenation and circulation, check capillary glucose immediately (give IV dextrose if low), obtain temperature, ECG, end-tidal CO₂, blood gas, electrolytes, CBC, toxicology when appropriate, and review sedatives, opioids and paralytics.
- Consider naloxone when opioid toxicity is plausible; do not routinely give flumazenil in mixed overdose or benzodiazepine-dependent patients because seizures may occur.
- Give thiamine early in malnutrition/alcohol dependence while correcting hypoglycaemia without delay.
- Sepsis, seizures including nonconvulsive status, stroke, trauma and CNS infection are simultaneous diagnostic priorities.

- A deteriorating patient with asymmetrical pupils, new lateralising signs, severe headache, trauma or anticoagulation warrants emergency noncontrast CT.
- Add CTA head/neck for suspected large vessel occlusion, aneurysm or dissection, with CT perfusion in selected stroke pathways.
- MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging is more sensitive for early/small infarction, brainstem stroke, encephalitis, hypoxic injury and diffuse axonal injury, but must not delay reperfusion or life-saving surgery.
- Continuous EEG is essential when seizure activity may be nonconvulsive.
- Lumbar puncture is contraindicated or deferred if mass effect, obstructive hydrocephalus, impending herniation or substantial coagulopathy is suspected.

## 2.2 Glasgow Coma Scale: record the components rather than a total alone

- The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) records best **eye (E4–1), verbal (V5–1) and motor (M6–1)** responses.
- Eye: spontaneous 4, to speech 3, to pressure 2, none 1. Verbal: oriented 5, confused 4, inappropriate words 3, incomprehensible sounds 2, none 1. Motor: obey commands 6, localises pain 5, normal withdrawal 4, abnormal flexion 3, extension 2, none 1. Total ranges 3–15, but use notation such as **E2 Vt M5** when intubated; a total derived by assigning 1 to an untestable verbal component is misleading.
- State whether responses are affected by sedation, neuromuscular blockade, hearing/language barrier, facial swelling or ocular injury.

- **Localising** is purposeful movement toward the source of a stimulus, distinct from simple withdrawal.
- Apply central and peripheral stimuli correctly, avoid repeated injurious stimulation, and compare both sides.
- Pupillary size/reactivity, cranial nerves, motor asymmetry, corneal and cough reflexes, tone, plantar responses, and ventilatory pattern help localise the lesion.
- A falling motor score or new pupil asymmetry is often more clinically valuable than a change in the GCS total.
- Document pre-sedation GCS and trend frequently.

## 2.3 A reproducible five-minute focal neurological examination

- Start with level of consciousness, orientation and language (aphasia versus dysarthria), then inspect pupils and visual fields.
- Ask the patient to track, assess gaze preference, facial symmetry and bulbar function.
- Check pronator drift, arm elevation for ten seconds, leg elevation for five seconds, distal movements and comparison of muscle groups.
- Evaluate gross sensation, coordination (finger–nose/heel–shin), neglect and gait only when safe.
- For an intubated patient use eye opening, pupillary response, visual threat if appropriate, gaze, command-following, limb motor symmetry and pain response.
- In an acute stroke use a structured National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS), which quantifies deficit but underestimates some posterior circulation symptoms.

- A cranial nerve examination also discriminates mass effect from a pharmacological pupil: third-nerve compression produces a dilated often poorly reactive pupil and ptosis/ocular motility impairment, whereas topical agents, ocular injury or prior surgery can alter pupils without neurological catastrophe.
- **Do not explain away a new fixed pupil in a deteriorating patient before imaging and treating raised ICP.**

## 2.4 Neuroimaging patterns that must be recognised promptly

| Disorder | Typical CT / vascular imaging appearance | Clinical implication |
|---|---|---|
| Epidural haematoma | Biconvex (lentiform) extra-axial high-density collection, limited by sutures; may accompany temporal bone fracture | Arterial expansion and uncal herniation; urgent neurosurgical evacuation when indicated |
| Acute subdural haematoma | Crescentic collection crossing sutures but limited by dural attachments, often with underlying brain injury | High mortality/secondary contusion and oedema; monitor midline shift and clinical state |
| Subarachnoid haemorrhage | Hyperdensity in basal cisterns, sylvian fissures or cortical sulci; aneurysm on CTA/DSA | Rebleeding, hydrocephalus and delayed cerebral ischaemia |
| Intraparenchymal haemorrhage | Focal hyperdense clot with oedema; deep basal ganglia/thalamic (hypertension) or lobar (including amyloid/structural lesions) | Haematoma expansion, ventricular extension, mass effect; controlled BP and anticoagulant reversal |
| Early ischaemic stroke | May be normal initially; loss of grey-white differentiation, insular ribbon loss, hyperdense artery; CTA occlusion | Time-critical IV thrombolysis/EVT decisions; ASPECTS estimates early MCA infarct burden |
| Diffuse axonal injury | CT may be relatively normal or show punctate shear haemorrhages at grey-white junction/corpus callosum; MRI SWI/DWI more sensitive | Explains disproportionate coma after deceleration injury |
| Hydrocephalus | Ventricular enlargement, transependymal CSF seepage and/or obstructing lesion | Neurosurgical CSF diversion; avoid LP if obstructive |
| Herniation | Effaced basal cisterns, midline shift, compressed ventricles, descending/tonsillar displacement | Immediate brain-rescue measures and surgical consultation |

- CTA identifies aneurysm, stenosis, dissection and arterial occlusion.
- Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) has high spatial/temporal resolution for aneurysms, vasospasm treatment and complex vascular lesions but carries invasive contrast/vascular risks.
- Transcranial Doppler (TCD) samples velocity, **not** flow directly; velocity rises with vasospasm but also with hyperdynamic circulation and anaemia, so interpret with symptoms and vessel ratios.

## 2.5 Delayed awakening or new deficit after anaesthesia/ICU sedation

- A postoperative patient who has not awakened has common pharmacological explanations (residual volatile/propofol, opioids, benzodiazepines, residual paralysis), but the dangerous mistake is to assume that every failure to wake is drug-related.
- Review anaesthesia record, blood loss, hypotension, hypoxaemia, embolic risks, glucose, CO₂, electrolytes, temperature and neuromuscular monitoring.
- Check pupils and focal signs immediately; obtain glucose, ABG and blood tests while reducing sedative confounding.
- If focal deficit, seizure or unexplained depressed consciousness persists, initiate stroke/neurosurgical pathways urgently, including imaging/CTA as indicated.
- The critical care patient who wakes weak on one side could have ischaemic stroke, haemorrhage, critical illness neuromyopathy, Todd paresis after a seizure or a spinal cord lesion; sensory pattern and cranial signs help distinguish these.

- After cardiac, vascular or major surgery, embolic ischaemic stroke, watershed infarction from hypoperfusion, air embolism and intracranial haemorrhage become particularly relevant.
- Intraoperative awareness and a patient who is awake but paralysed are different problems from coma.
- Confirm neuromuscular recovery using quantitative train-of-four, review potential pseudocholinesterase deficiency and consider residual sedatives before escalating to neuroimaging, but **do not wait for all drugs to wear off when an asymmetry is present**.

## 2.6 When a new postoperative deficit localises to the spinal cord, nerve or brain

- An unexpected focal deficit after anaesthesia is a diagnosis requiring anatomical localisation before attributing it to drugs, positioning or a regional block.
- **Cortical signs** (aphasia, neglect, gaze deviation, homonymous hemianopia) favour cerebral stroke
- A sensory level, bilateral leg weakness, urinary retention or saddle anaesthesia raises spinal cord/cauda equina compression
- A single nerve distribution with preserved cranial function suggests peripheral injury.
- These distinctions guide the first scan, but time-sensitive evaluation must run in parallel.

**First 10 minutes:**

- Record last known normal, vital signs, blood glucose, pupils, GCS/NIHSS or appropriate cord/limb examination, anticoagulant and neuraxial procedure details.
- Correct hypoxaemia, marked hypotension and metabolic disturbance.
- Review quantitative neuromuscular recovery and residual drugs without allowing this to delay emergency imaging if lateralising signs or cord red flags are present.
- Activate a stroke call for a suspected cerebral event and obtain immediate noncontrast CT with CT angiography for potential large-vessel occlusion; MRI diffusion may be needed when CT is negative and clinical suspicion persists.
- Document the deficit before any further sedation.

- **After neuraxial instrumentation or spinal surgery**, severe new back pain, radicular symptoms, progressive weakness or bladder/bowel dysfunction may reflect spinal epidural haematoma, abscess or direct injury.
- Stop a running epidural infusion so a dense local-anaesthetic block does not mask evolution; contact anaesthesia, neurosurgery/spinal surgery and radiology immediately.
- Arrange urgent **MRI of the relevant spine** (CT if MRI is genuinely unavailable) while preparing intervention.
- Neurological deterioration caused by a compressive postoperative haematoma is a surgical emergency: outcome worsens with delay, and imaging should not create an avoidable barrier to decompression in a clinically unmistakable rapidly progressing case.
- Assess and correct anticoagulation but do not delay specialist contact while waiting for laboratory results.

- Other important mimics include Todd paresis, nonconvulsive status, hypoglycaemia, hypercapnia, local anaesthetic toxicity, acute functional neurological symptoms and peripheral nerve compression.
- A presumed peripheral injury needs examination of power, reflexes and sensory territory, follow-up and sometimes EMG/nerve-conduction studies; a suspected stroke or spinal compression cannot be safely diagnosed by exclusion alone.
- **Reassessment** matters: repeat and document observations, preserve a clear timeline, and communicate critical deterioration during transfer or handover.

items.body:
## 3.1 From a focal insult to secondary brain injury

- Primary injury is the instantaneous tissue disruption caused by impact, haemorrhage or ischaemia.
- **Secondary injury** is subsequent tissue damage driven by loss of perfusion, hypoxaemia, raised ICP, excitotoxicity, inflammation, seizures, disordered glucose control, fever, anaemia, coagulopathy and systemic complications.
- Whereas primary injury is largely complete when the patient reaches hospital, secondary injury is an important target of anaesthesia and intensive care.
- Cerebral hypoxia and hypotension should not be dismissed as brief reversible abnormalities: both predict worse functional outcomes after TBI.

- The injured brain has less autoregulatory reserve, so cerebral perfusion may become pressure dependent.
- Poor perfusion causes ischaemia and cellular oedema; oedema raises ICP, which lowers CPP and further reduces flow.
- A haemorrhagic contusion may enlarge during the first hours, especially with anticoagulation, and an initial CT does not guarantee stability.
- A comprehensive management plan must simultaneously control intracranial volume, preserve oxygen delivery, correct coagulation and search for an operable mass.

## 3.2 Which neurological patients require ICU and invasive monitoring?

- Patients with severe TBI (often GCS 3–8 after initial resuscitation), evolving CT abnormalities, pupillary or motor deterioration, mass lesions, hydrocephalus, severe SAH, refractory status epilepticus or acute postoperative neurological deterioration need neurocritical expertise.
- Classic Brain Trauma Foundation guidance supports ICP monitoring in salvageable severe TBI with an abnormal CT, and in selected severe TBI with normal CT plus high-risk features (age >40, motor posturing or hypotension).
- These criteria guide rather than replace specialist decisions.
- Monitoring is useful only if findings are acted on, and avoiding delayed surgery takes precedence over obtaining a monitor.

### Methods of intracranial monitoring

- An **EVD** enters a cerebral ventricle and measures ventricular pressure when closed to drainage; it permits therapeutic drainage, sampling and treatment of hydrocephalus.
- It requires a levelled system, typically referenced to the external auditory meatus/tragus as a surrogate of the foramen of Monro.
- The clinician prescribes drainage height (for example 10–15 cmH₂O above the reference) and whether drainage is continuous or intermittent; a drain that is open does not provide a reliable instantaneous ICP reading.
- Transducer level changes with patient position, so re-level after every repositioning.
- Overdrainage may cause ventricular collapse, catheter obstruction, subdural bleeding or herniation in selected mass lesions.
- Infection, intraventricular bleeding, dislodgement and occlusion are important complications.

- An **intraparenchymal fibreoptic or strain-gauge probe** permits continuous regional pressure readings and may be simpler to insert in compressed ventricles.
- It cannot drain CSF and some sensors drift without convenient recalibration.
- Epidural/subdural monitors are less reliable for global pressure.
- ICP is not always uniform in the injured cranium: an isolated regional measurement should be integrated with pupils, CT and neurological trajectory.
- Additional methods include brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO₂), EEG, TCD, jugular bulb saturation, cerebral microdialysis and autoregulation indices.
- Their utility depends on specialist expertise and a response plan; no single monitor replaces examination and imaging.

ICP waveforms have cardiac components P1 (percussion), P2 (tidal/compliance), P3 (dicrotic). An increased P2 relative to P1 may suggest deteriorating intracranial compliance but is neither sufficiently specific nor sufficient alone to trigger treatment. Plateau waves signal reduced intracranial compliance and should prompt assessment of CPP and reversible triggers.

## 3.3 The immediate response to suspected herniation or an ICP crisis

- Treat sudden anisocoria, extensor posturing, rapidly falling GCS, bradycardia/hypertension (a late Cushing response), or sustained ICP elevation as life-threatening deterioration.
- Call the neurosurgeon and senior neurointensivist; assess and treat while arranging immediate imaging or theatre.
- Confirm there is not hypoxaemia, hypotension, hypercapnia, seizure, coughing, ventilator dyssynchrony, obstructed venous drainage, catheter malfunction or a new surgical clot.

- **Practical sequence:**

- **1.** Stabilise oxygenation and haemodynamics; avoid saturations below normal and maintain adequate MAP at brain level. Check glucose, temperature, PaCO₂, sodium and haemoglobin. Correct seizures or agitation.
- **2.** Position head about 30° up, neutral and free from neck compression; ensure venous drainage. Adequate analgesia/sedation reduces coughing and metabolic demand. If an EVD exists, check its level and patency and drain CSF according to the prescribed order.
- **3.** For an ICP crisis use **hyperosmolar therapy** while preparing definitive treatment: hypertonic saline (e.g. 3% NaCl 2–3 mL/kg IV, or locally specified 23.4% 30 mL via appropriate central access) or mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg IV.
  - These are example rescue regimens rather than interchangeable routine prescriptions.
  - Mannitol causes osmotic diuresis, hypovolaemia and hypotension; hypertonic saline raises serum sodium/chloride and may provoke hyperchloraemic acidosis.
  - Monitor serum sodium, osmolality, kidney function and volume state; avoid uncontrolled cumulative hyperosmolar therapy.
  - Local concentration, line access and maximum sodium protocols take precedence.
- **4.** If impending herniation persists while awaiting surgery, **brief controlled hyperventilation** may reduce PaCO₂ to approximately 30–35 mmHg as a rescue bridge, returning toward normocapnia after definitive control. Prolonged marked hypocapnia is dangerous because it reduces CBF, particularly early after injury.
- **5.** Obtain urgent CT and definitive treatment: haematoma evacuation, decompressive surgery, EVD for obstructive hydrocephalus, or other specific intervention.
  - Refractory elevated ICP may require deeper sedation, further osmotherapy, neuromuscular blockade to control triggering, barbiturate therapy, selected decompression or targeted temperature management within specialist care.

**Important distinction:**

- A lower numerical ICP is not equivalent to a better neurological outcome.
- RESCUEicp showed decompressive craniectomy for refractory raised ICP reduced mortality but increased survival with severe disability and vegetative outcomes at six months; functional results must be discussed sensitively and interpreted across longer follow-up.
- DECRA found that very early bifrontal decompression for diffuse injury and less severe ICP thresholds did not improve functional outcomes.
- Patient selection and family-centred outcome preferences matter.

## 3.4 Severe TBI resuscitation and ICU management

- At presentation, the priority is simultaneous trauma resuscitation with cervical spine protection, recognition of life-threatening extracranial haemorrhage, and prevention of cerebral hypoxia/hypotension.
- Intubate if the airway is not protected, severe agitation prevents safe care, or oxygenation/ventilation is failing; severe TBI (GCS ≤8) is a common indication but not a substitute for assessing airway reflexes and trajectory.
- Use a haemodynamically appropriate induction (e.g. titrated ketamine or etomidate where available, or carefully adjusted propofol), neuromuscular blockade and active vasopressor support.
- Avoid a large post-induction fall in MAP.
- Preoxygenation and a gentle laryngoscopy protect against episodes of hypoxaemia, sympathetic surges and aspiration.

- TBI blood-pressure objectives must consider age and individual injury.
- Brain Trauma Foundation level-III thresholds propose SBP ≥100 mmHg at age 50–69 and ≥110 mmHg at age 15–49 or >70.
- These are **minimum avoidance thresholds**, not adequate goals for every patient; when ICP is elevated, target CPP usually 60–70 mmHg and avoid routinely driving CPP above 70 using large fluid and vasopressor loads.
- Treatment is generally recommended for sustained ICP >22 mmHg, interpreted with imaging and examination.
- Fever prevention, glucose control without hypoglycaemia, euvolaemia, isotonic fluids, avoidance of hyponatraemia, prevention of hypoxaemia and timely control of intracranial lesions are central.

- Ventilate with lung-protective tidal volumes based on predicted body weight, aiming for normoxaemia and normocapnia.
- ARDS may require PEEP or prone positioning despite ICP concerns; assess cerebral response rather than denying essential lung support.
- Sedation is often propofol with opioid analgesia because of titratability and favourable cerebral metabolic effects; prolonged high-dose propofol can cause infusion syndrome and haemodynamic compromise.
- Dexmedetomidine may assist lighter sedation but does not replace seizure control or deep sedation when medically necessary.
- A sedation interruption may be unsafe in unstable intracranial hypertension; when safe, serial examinations are invaluable.

- Prevent secondary insults with adequate nutrition (start enteral feeding once appropriate), pressure-area care, VTE prophylaxis using mechanical and then pharmacological methods after haemorrhage stability and neurosurgical review, infection prevention, mobilisation/rehabilitation and early family communication.
- Routine prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated for all closed TBI.
- Antiseizure prophylaxis may reduce early (within seven days) post-traumatic seizures in selected severe TBI but does not prevent late epilepsy and should not routinely be prolonged.
- Avoid corticosteroids in severe TBI: CRASH showed increased mortality with high-dose methylprednisolone.
- Tranexamic acid may have a role in selected mild–moderate head injury early after trauma (CRASH-3 subgroup findings), but it is not a substitute for standard haemorrhage and neurosurgical care.

### Bedside physiology example

- A 30-year-old with contusions has MAP 75 mmHg, ICP 28 mmHg, PaCO₂ 51 mmHg and fever 39°C.
- CPP is approximately 47 mmHg. Merely giving mannitol and ignoring MAP, hypercapnia and temperature is incomplete.
- Correct ventilatory failure toward normocapnia, treat fever and agitation, optimise MAP/volume state and check EVD/CT.
- A targeted osmotic bolus may reduce ICP quickly, while surgical review determines whether swelling or an evolving clot is responsible.
- Recalculate CPP and judge the neurological response rather than focusing on one number.

## 3.5 Evidence and contested choices in traumatic brain injury

- The management of severe TBI involves important differences between **physiological control** and **proven functional benefit**.
- The Brain Trauma Foundation ICP treatment threshold of >22 mmHg and CPP target 60–70 mmHg provide a workable framework, but neither implies that every patient should be treated identically.
- An older patient with impaired autoregulation, anaemia and hypoxaemia may suffer ischaemia despite a CPP of 65 mmHg, while fluid/pressor-driven CPP of 85 mmHg may produce lung injury in another.
- When advanced monitoring is available, clinicians sometimes use pressure reactivity (PRx), brain tissue oxygen and other data to individualise perfusion, although routine superiority of every multimodal strategy over high-quality standard care is not established.

**Transfusion illustrates this uncertainty:**

- The 2024 **HEMOTION** trial randomised 742 moderate/severe TBI patients with anaemia to a liberal transfusion threshold of Hb ≤100 g/L versus a restrictive Hb ≤70 g/L.
- Unfavourable six-month neurological outcome occurred in 68.4% versus 73.5% of evaluable patients respectively, with a confidence interval crossing no effect; the primary result did not establish superiority of liberal transfusion.
- A rigid instruction to transfuse all TBI patients above 100 g/L is therefore unsupported.
- Consider Hb, active bleeding, cerebral oxygen delivery, coronary disease, neurological deterioration and transfusion harms together.
- The trial is different from general ICU trials and should be mentioned when discussing anaemia management.

**Decompressive surgery should be framed as a value-sensitive rescue treatment:**

- Removing skull bone improves compliance and can control refractory ICP, but the benefit may be survival with profound disability rather than a return to independence.
- Explain the difference between reducing mortality and improving the proportion of neurologically intact survivors.
- The **CRASH corticosteroid trial** changed practice by demonstrating excess mortality with high-dose steroids, and **DECRA/RESCUEicp** remind us that anatomical decompression does not automatically restore neuronal function.
- The purpose of TBI care is not simply ‘normal ICP’: it is preservation of tissue and a patient-centred outcome.

- Other treatment controversies include prophylactic hypothermia (cooling can reduce ICP but has not consistently improved outcome and may increase complications), prophylactic antiepileptic choice (early seizure reduction is not prevention of post-traumatic epilepsy), and timing of VTE prophylaxis.
- Early mechanical prophylaxis is appropriate in many patients, but pharmacological prophylaxis depends on stable haemorrhage and repeat imaging/neurosurgical advice.
- A blanket delay of several weeks may expose patients to avoidable PE, while immediate anticoagulation in an expanding intracranial bleed is unsafe.
- Regular neurological examination, targeted imaging, multidisciplinary review and rehabilitation remain the unglamorous foundation of good care.

## 3.6 What changes when an anaesthetised patient develops raised ICP?

Suspected intraoperative ICP elevation is assessed with the same causal framework:

- Airway obstruction or hypoventilation → hypercapnia → cerebral vasodilatation.
- High PEEP or jugular compression → impaired venous drainage.
- Hypertension/tachycardia → inadequate depth or autonomic response.
- Intracranial haemorrhage or surgical obstruction → new space-occupying pathology.

- Verify capnography against ABG, examine positioning, discuss operative conditions and pupil/neuromonitor findings, deepen analgesia/sedation if appropriate, and maintain cerebral perfusion during temporising therapy.
- Pupil change, refractory swelling or catastrophic bleeding demands immediate surgical response.
- Hyperventilation, osmotherapy and CSF drainage are **bridges to definitive cause-directed treatment**.

## 3.7 Individualising the neurocritical care plan: what ICP and CPP targets cannot tell you

- Treating sustained ICP above 22 mmHg and usually targeting CPP 60–70 mmHg provides a common framework, but **the pressure number is a surrogate rather than the injury itself**.
- An EVD may show a satisfactory pressure while a local contusion remains ischaemic; a higher ICP transiently during suctioning is not equivalent to persistent pressure elevation with poor perfusion.
- Correlate duration and burden of elevation with examination, repeat imaging, ventricular size, sodium, haemodynamics, temperature, oxygenation and EEG.

- Whenever CPP is calculated, specify the level at which MAP is referenced.
- A patient positioned at 30° with a transducer zeroed at the heart can appear to have adequate CPP while the true arterial pressure at the circle of Willis is materially lower.
- Review the relationship between head position, venous return and systemic blood pressure before escalating to more vasopressor.
- Conversely, routinely forcing CPP above 70 mmHg may increase lung injury through vasopressor/fluid burden without proven neurological gain.

- **Advanced monitoring** is adjunctive.
- Brain tissue oxygen monitoring measures local oxygen tension, often targeting avoidance of sustained PbtO₂ below about 20 mmHg in programmes that use it; low values require investigation of oxygenation, haemoglobin, CPP, ventilation and local lesion position.
- Transcranial Doppler estimates vascular velocity rather than directly measuring cerebral blood flow.
- Continuous EEG is particularly useful when paralytics or sedatives obscure seizures.
- Cerebral microdialysis may identify metabolic crisis (for example raised lactate/pyruvate ratio), but its invasive sampling and interpretation remain specialised.
- Describe what each variable actually measures before suggesting a treatment.

- Hyperosmolar treatment requires distinction between **rescue boluses** for herniation and repeated treatment of documented ICP elevation.
- Mannitol can reduce intravascular volume and precipitate hypotension; hypertonic saline can worsen hypernatraemia, hyperchloraemia or volume overload.
- Serial osmolality, sodium/chloride, fluid balance and kidney function are therefore mechanistically necessary.
- Neither agent has demonstrated a universal long-term functional outcome advantage over the other.
- Avoid glucose-containing hypotonic maintenance fluids in an unstable oedematous brain, but equally avoid treating every sodium value with prophylactic severe hypernatraemia.

- Neurological outcome and goals of care must not be inferred from a single ICP, GCS or early postoperative scan.
- The DECRA and RESCUEicp populations differed by timing, refractory ICP definitions and surgical strategies; survival benefits may be coupled with survival with dependency.
- Discuss anticipated functional outcomes and uncertainty with the multidisciplinary team and family, while providing rehabilitation, swallowing and pressure-injury prevention early enough to limit preventable disability.

items.title: 4. Acute ischaemic stroke: reperfusion, brain rescue and perioperative implications
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 4.1 Stroke recognition and the importance of time

- A thrombus may form over atherosclerotic plaque, embolise from atrial fibrillation or a cardiac source, or occlude a small penetrating artery.
- Cervical artery dissection, vasculitis, paradoxical embolism and perioperative emboli are less common possibilities.
- Core infarction develops as flow fails; surrounding collateral-dependent penumbra remains salvageable for a variable interval.
- The traditional distinction between a narrow ‘time window’ and an expanded ‘tissue window’ reflects modern CT/MR vascular and perfusion imaging: some patients remain suitable for reperfusion at 24 hours, while others develop large infarcts rapidly.
- **Last known well** and symptom severity/disability must be established immediately.

- Use a stroke call pathway, check glucose, oxygenation, blood pressure, temperature, last anticoagulant dose, platelet/coagulation state and baseline functional status.
- Obtain immediate noncontrast head CT to exclude haemorrhage and CTA head/neck to identify large-vessel occlusion.
- Perfusion imaging or MRI may be used in delayed, wake-up or selected borderline cases but should not delay treatment in standard candidates.
- Maintain safe swallowing precautions and avoid aspiration until screening.
- A patient with aphasia, hemianopia, neglect or brainstem signs may have disabling stroke despite relatively preserved limb power.

## 4.2 IV thrombolysis: eligibility, drug, dose and physiological goals

- The **2026 AHA/ASA guideline** recommends either tenecteplase **0.25 mg/kg IV bolus, maximum 25 mg** or alteplase **0.9 mg/kg IV, maximum 90 mg (10% bolus, remainder over one hour)** in eligible adults within 4.5 hours.
- Tenecteplase 0.4 mg/kg is not the recommended stroke dose.
- Thrombolysis requires a disabling deficit and exclusion of major contraindications such as active intracranial bleeding, certain recent neurosurgical procedures, uncontrolled severe hypertension, and relevant anticoagulant effects.
- Anticoagulant-specific pathways are nuanced: a medication list alone does not establish whether thrombolysis is safe, and specialist review with drug timing, renal function or specific assays is essential.
- Minor **non-disabling** stroke is usually not thrombolysed.

- Before IV thrombolysis lower BP if necessary to **<185/110 mmHg**; for the subsequent 24 hours aim for **≤180/105 mmHg** with frequent neurological/BP checks and avoidance of hypotension.
- After IVT, antiplatelets and anticoagulants are generally deferred until repeat CT/MRI at approximately 24 hours has excluded bleeding.
- Watch for symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (neurological deterioration, headache, hypertension, vomiting) and orolingual angioedema, particularly with ACE inhibitors.
- Stop the infusion if alteplase is running, activate the stroke bleeding protocol and rapidly assess with CT/coagulation studies; manage reversal and fibrinogen replacement with stroke/haematology specialists.

Selected imaging-defined patients presenting 4.5–9 hours from last known well or with wake-up stroke may benefit from IVT based on salvageable tissue; this is a specialist imaging protocol, not routine time-based eligibility. Rapid reperfusion should not be delayed by elaborate additional studies when standard criteria already establish candidacy.

## 4.3 Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT)

- EVT physically removes proximal intracranial thrombus using aspiration or stent-retriever systems.
- For appropriate anterior circulation ICA/M1 occlusions, EVT is strongly supported within six hours and, in imaging-selected patients, up to 24 hours.
- Modern trials have broadened eligibility to selected **large-core infarcts** (e.g. ASPECTS 3–5) rather than excluding everyone with an extensive early CT change.
- Basilar artery occlusion may also benefit from EVT within 24 hours in suitable patients, particularly with substantial clinical deficit and limited established injury.
- EVT should not be withheld solely because the patient has received IV thrombolysis; if both are indicated, expedite both without waiting for a response to IVT.

- Anaesthesia for EVT is individualised.
- General anaesthesia is indicated for airway compromise, severe agitation, reduced consciousness, vomiting or inability to remain motionless; monitored care may be suitable for a cooperative patient.
- Both can have acceptable outcomes if **hypotension and delays are avoided**.
- Ensure rapid access, a robust blood-pressure plan, arterial monitoring when feasible without delaying puncture, normoxia, normocapnia, appropriate glucose and smooth emergence.
- The goal is stable collateral perfusion before recanalisation and avoidance of reperfusion injury afterwards.

**Post-EVT BP:**

- Avoid automatically targeting SBP <140 mmHg after technically successful reperfusion.
- Recent trials and the 2026 guideline show that intensive post-EVT lowering to <140 mmHg can be harmful.
- Individualise with the stroke/interventional team, haemorrhagic transformation risk, residual stenosis, collateral dependence and other diseases.
- Large infarction can develop malignant oedema despite successful vessel reopening.
- Monitor for reperfusion haemorrhage, infarct progression, cerebral oedema, seizures, aspiration, contrast nephrotoxicity and groin/radial access complications.

## 4.4 Patients not receiving reperfusion

- Absent IVT/EVT or another hypertensive emergency, permissive hypertension supports collateral flow.
- For BP **<220/120 mmHg**, routine early reduction within the first 48–72 hours is generally not beneficial; if persistently above this threshold or with concomitant aortic dissection, cardiac failure or hypertensive encephalopathy, cautiously reduce and individualise (often initial ≈15% reduction rather than abrupt normalisation).
- Treat hypotension, dehydration, hypoxia, fever and hypoglycaemia.
- Aspirin is generally introduced within 24–48 hours after non-haemorrhagic ischaemic stroke when not thrombolysed; selected minor non-cardioembolic stroke/high-risk TIA may receive a short (≈21-day) course of dual antiplatelet therapy after appropriate assessment.
- Anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation is initiated at a time influenced by infarct size, haemorrhagic transformation and current evidence, not automatically on day one in all strokes.

- For malignant MCA infarction or cerebellar swelling, early neurosurgical decompression may prevent herniation, though disability outcomes and age/functional status influence the decision.
- Large cerebellar infarction with fourth-ventricle compression can require posterior fossa decompression; an EVD alone may be insufficient.
- Monitor serial neurological examination, consciousness and CT when deterioration occurs.
- Aspiration prevention, early rehabilitation and VTE prevention are fundamental throughout.

## 4.5 Worked blood-pressure decisions after acute ischaemic stroke

- The physiological reason different stroke treatments require different BP plans is **collateral dependence before reperfusion** versus **haemorrhagic and hyperperfusion risk after reperfusion**.
- An occluded MCA receives partial collateral flow from neighbouring territories; abrupt reduction of systemic BP can reduce penumbral flow below its critical threshold.
- After IVT, excess pressure may exacerbate haemorrhagic transformation.
- After successful EVT, intensive reduction to very low targets has proved harmful even though the vessel is open, probably because microvascular dysfunction and residual infarct remain vulnerable.

| Situation | General approach | Why it is different |
|---|---|---|
| AIS candidate for IVT | Reduce BP below 185/110 mmHg before treatment; use protocol-controlled IV agent | Severe hypertension raises thrombolytic bleeding risk |
| First 24 h after IVT | Keep ≤180/105 mmHg; frequent examinations and monitoring | Haemorrhagic transformation risk; avoid excessive fall |
| AIS without reperfusion | If BP <220/120 and no other emergency, often avoid early routine lowering | Preserves collateral perfusion of the penumbra |
| Successfully reperfused EVT | Avoid intensive SBP <140 as routine; team-specific target | 2026 guideline identifies harm with aggressive lowering |
| Cerebral oedema/herniation | Prioritise CPP and neurosurgical treatment over generic stroke BP chart | Pressure may be required to perfuse the compressed brain |

- In addition to blood pressure, the strongest avoidable secondary insults include aspiration pneumonia, fever, hypoglycaemia and missed cerebral oedema.
- The 2026 AHA guideline specifically advises **against intensive insulin targeting 80–130 mg/dL**, which increases severe hypoglycaemia without improving outcome.
- Maintain a reasonable inpatient glucose range according to institutional protocol rather than treating mildly elevated glucose with high-risk tight infusions.
- Do not give routine prophylactic antibiotics to all stroke patients, but screen swallowing early and treat proven infection.

- Thrombolysis and thrombectomy change anaesthetic practice beyond the stroke unit.
- If surgery is immediately necessary after IVT or when an intracranial stent is deployed, antithrombotic effects and access-site bleeding require coordination.
- New neurological deterioration after EVT may reflect **re-occlusion, intracranial haemorrhage, malignant oedema or seizure**.
- The correct response is rapid re-evaluation and CT/CTA rather than attributing it to a normal reperfusion phenomenon.

## 4.6 Preoperative assessment in the patient with prior cerebrovascular disease

- A previous stroke raises perioperative stroke, myocardial infarction, delirium and mortality risk because of atherosclerotic disease, reduced physiological reserve and residual cerebral perfusion vulnerability.
- Determine stroke type, date, cause, degree of recovery, carotid stenosis, AF, antiplatelets/anticoagulants, residual swallowing and cognitive impairment, and current function.
- Evaluate whether elective surgery can be delayed after a recent stroke; contemporary guidance often considers **at least three months** after stroke for non-urgent surgery when feasible, but time must be balanced against surgical urgency, neurological trajectory and the indication.
- This is not an absolute safe/unsafe threshold.
- Carotid intervention is reserved for appropriate symptomatic stenosis, not a routine prerequisite to unrelated surgery.

- During surgery avoid hypotension relative to the patient’s usual perfusion pressure, excessive fluctuations in CO₂, hypoxia, anaemia and major glucose disturbances.
- Manage antithrombotic therapy based on indication (recent coronary stent, AF, secondary prevention), procedure bleeding risk and neuraxial constraints.
- Perioperative new neurological deficit is a **time-critical stroke alert**, not automatically postoperative delirium.
- Document a focused baseline before sedation, investigate promptly, and recognise that recent surgery or neuraxial procedures may restrict IV thrombolysis even when EVT remains an option.

## 4.7 Elective and urgent surgery after a previous stroke or TIA

- A history of cerebrovascular disease changes perioperative risk because cerebral autoregulation may be impaired, vascular disease is often systemic, and withholding antithrombotic therapy may precipitate embolic events.
- Determine **stroke type, mechanism, date, residual disability, progression, antithrombotic indication, carotid disease and current neurological baseline** before deciding that a patient is optimised.
- An apparently minor TIA may represent symptomatic carotid stenosis requiring urgent vascular investigation rather than routine pre-admission clearance.

- The 2024 ACC/AHA perioperative guideline, retained in the 2026 update, considers it reasonable to defer **elective noncardiac surgery for at least three months after stroke or TIA**, when possible.
- This is not an absolute ban for urgent cancer or limb-saving surgery: compare risk of neurological harm from proceeding against harm from delay, and agree a plan with the relevant specialties.
- Earlier observational studies suggested six to nine months; more recent data found much of the reduction in excess perioperative stroke risk occurred by around 90 days.
- Do not present either interval as a guarantee of safety.

- Preoperative investigation should be directed by the clinical question.
- Review brain/vascular imaging and carotid ultrasound or CTA for symptomatic disease when management would change.
- Examine AF and cardiac embolic risks, blood pressure, diabetes, lipids, functional capacity, dysphagia and capacity to consent.
- Continue usual vascular risk reduction; individualise aspirin, P2Y12 inhibition and anticoagulation according to indication, time since coronary/vascular intervention, surgery bleeding risk and regional-anaesthesia restrictions.
- Routine bridging with therapeutic heparin for most AF patients is usually more harmful than helpful, but recent mechanical valves or other very-high-risk indications require individual planning.

- Intraoperatively maintain cerebral oxygen delivery by avoiding prolonged hypotension, hypoxaemia, severe anaemia, marked hypocapnia and glycaemic extremes.
- Use the patient’s usual BP and vascular reserve to individualise targets rather than selecting an arbitrary universal MAP.
- Re-establish baseline neurology before sedative premedication where practical.
- Neither volatile nor TIVA techniques reliably eliminates perioperative stroke risk.
- Postoperatively provide prompt recovery examination, aspiration/dysphagia precautions, AF recognition and early reinstatement of antithrombotics when haemostasis permits; any new deficit activates an immediate stroke pathway.

items.title: 5. Intracranial haemorrhage: anatomy, physiology and emergency management
items.body:
## 5.1 Clinical differences between the bleeding syndromes

- Intracranial blood is both a mass and a potent cause of secondary injury.
- **Epidural haematoma** typically results from meningeal arterial injury associated with fracture, often temporal; a transient lucid interval is classic but not required.
- A rapidly enlarging lens-shaped collection can compress the temporal lobe and third nerve.
- **Subdural haematoma** reflects tearing of bridging veins and frequently coexists with severe parenchymal injury; anticoagulation, age and cerebral atrophy increase vulnerability.
- **Intraparenchymal haemorrhage (ICH)** results from hypertensive small-vessel pathology, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, anticoagulation, vascular malformation, tumour or trauma.
- **SAH** from ruptured aneurysm commonly presents as a sudden thunderclap headache with meningism, vomiting or collapse; it is addressed separately in Chapter 6. Intraventricular haemorrhage causes obstructive hydrocephalus and can accompany ICH or SAH.

- The natural history differs.
- Epidural clots can cause precipitous early deterioration, subdural injury has additional delayed oedema and contusion evolution, and primary ICH often expands within the first hours.
- A chronic subdural collection may present over weeks with headache, fluctuating confusion, focal deficits or falls.
- A patient who initially appears stable may therefore require repeat imaging and serial neurological observations based on the type of lesion, neurological status and anticoagulation.

## 5.2 Initial resuscitation of intracranial bleeding

- Secure ABCs and avoid hypoxaemia, hypotension and excessive rises in ICP.
- Perform rapid GCS/pupillary examination, CT/CTA as indicated, coagulation studies, platelet count, fibrinogen, medication review and blood-group preparation.
- Contact neurosurgery early for evacuable clot, hydrocephalus, brainstem compression or deterioration.
- Consider reversal of anticoagulation as an emergency rather than deferring until surgical decisions have been made.

- In **mild–moderate spontaneous ICH** presenting with SBP 150–220 mmHg, smooth early reduction toward approximately **140 mmHg**, maintaining roughly **130–150 mmHg**, is supported by the 2022 AHA/ASA guideline; actively driving SBP **below 130 mmHg** may be harmful.
- These parameters should not be applied uncritically to massive ICH with compromised CPP, herniation or surgical decompression: cerebral perfusion takes priority and requires tailored MAP/ICP management.
- IV nicardipine, clevidipine or labetalol are typical options according to availability and cardiac physiology.
- Avoid large rapid swings.

### Anticoagulant reversal in life-threatening intracranial haemorrhage

| Agent | Core reversal strategy | Important caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Warfarin | Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) with **IV vitamin K** (often 5–10 mg) | PCC rapidly replaces factors; vitamin K sustains reversal; recheck INR |
| Dabigatran | Idarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5-g doses) | Rebound anticoagulant effect may occur with severe renal dysfunction; re-evaluate |
| Apixaban/rivaroxaban/edoxaban | Specific factor Xa reversal agent if available/appropriate, or 4F-PCC under local protocol | Agent availability, thrombosis risk, timing and anti-Xa assay modify plan |
| Unfractionated heparin | Protamine guided by recent heparin dose (commonly ≈1 mg/100 units heparin, maximum per local protocol) | Excess protamine itself impairs coagulation; monitor ACT/aPTT |
| LMWH | Protamine provides partial anti-Xa reversal; haematology input | Effect depends on drug, dose and timing |
| Antiplatelet therapy | Stop relevant agents and consider specialist-directed interventions in selected surgical contexts | Routine platelet transfusion in spontaneous ICH without emergency surgery can worsen outcomes (PATCH) |

- Reverse while preparing urgent surgery if appropriate.
- Desmopressin may be considered in selected antiplatelet-associated ICH or urgent neurosurgery but evidence is uncertain and not routine universal therapy.
- Maintain normothermia, ionised calcium, adequate haemoglobin and fibrinogen when bleeding is substantial.
- Correct coagulopathy with mechanism-guided therapy rather than reflex massive transfusion for every spontaneous haemorrhage.

## 5.3 The modern evidence behind intracerebral haemorrhage care bundles

- A patient with spontaneous ICH deteriorates not only because of clot volume.
- Ongoing bleeding expands the mass, perihaematomal oedema evolves, coagulopathy sustains expansion, glucose extremes impair tissue and fever increases metabolic demand.
- The **INTERACT3** trial tested a coordinated care bundle emphasising early BP control, glucose management, fever treatment and rapid reversal of warfarin-related coagulopathy; it supported improvement in functional recovery in a broad ICH population.
- It is misleading to interpret the bundle as proof that extreme glucose targets or indiscriminate BP lowering to below 130 mmHg are beneficial in every individual.
- The practical teaching is the importance of timely, coordinated correction of multiple physiological insults, avoiding both undertreatment and overshoot.

**Surgery has become more nuanced:**

- Traditional STICH trials found no universal benefit of open surgery for all supratentorial ICH.
- In the **2024 ENRICH trial**, early minimally invasive evacuation in a selected population with a lobar or anterior basal ganglia haemorrhage of 30–80 mL improved an overall utility-weighted functional outcome measure, with apparent benefit driven mainly by lobar cases.
- This is not a mandate to evacuate every hypertensive basal ganglia haemorrhage.
- Site, volume, time, neurological status, degree of mass effect, patient priorities and local expertise determine candidacy.
- Posterior fossa clot with hydrocephalus or brainstem compression remains a different, often urgent surgical indication.

- For suspected **cerebral amyloid angiopathy**, recurrent lobar bleeds in older adults and MRI microbleeds/superficial siderosis are clues; risk of future ICH affects antithrombotic decisions.
- Deep haemorrhage associated with hypertension, lobar haemorrhage related to anticoagulation/amyloid, and traumatic contusion may have similar CT density but require different recurrence prevention.
- CTA ‘spot sign’ of contrast extravasation predicts expansion risk but does not replace serial neurological assessment or determine every surgical decision.

## 5.4 Operative versus nonoperative strategies

- Epidural and acute subdural evacuation depends on clot dimensions, midline shift, neurological state and pupillary signs; widely used traumatic neurosurgical thresholds include epidural haematoma >30 cm³ and acute subdural thickness >10 mm or midline shift >5 mm regardless of GCS, but **emergency deterioration overrides size rules**.
- For spontaneous supratentorial ICH, routine open craniotomy has not consistently improved outcomes; selected patients may benefit from minimally invasive evacuation or decompression, especially with life-threatening mass effect.
- Cerebellar haemorrhage causing neurological deterioration, brainstem compression, obstructive hydrocephalus or larger volume is an urgent surgical problem.
- An EVD may be required for intraventricular blood/hydrocephalus but can be insufficient in posterior fossa compression.

- Examine frequently for falling GCS, worsening asymmetry or seizures.
- Provide analgesia without masking examinations, controlled ventilation, VTE prophylaxis when safe, nutrition, swallowing assessment and multidisciplinary rehabilitation.
- Discuss prognostic uncertainty: early outcome scores should not be the sole basis for withdrawal decisions, especially while sedatives, seizures and potentially reversible hydrocephalus confound examination.

## 5.5 Focused 2026 update: antithrombotic-associated intracranial haemorrhage

- Reversal recommendations have evolved since the 2022 spontaneous ICH guideline.
- A **September 2026 Neurocritical Care Society/SCCM focused update** conditionally suggests **4-factor PCC rather than andexanet alfa** for oral factor-Xa-inhibitor-associated spontaneous ICH (moderate-certainty evidence) and traumatic ICH (very-low-certainty evidence).
- The distinction is important: andexanet improves haemostatic efficacy in some comparisons but has clinically relevant thrombotic risk; availability, timing, local protocols and specialist assessment remain decisive.
- Do not teach a specific factor-Xa reversal product as universally preferred without stating the guideline and jurisdiction.

- For warfarin-associated critical ICH, rapid factor replacement with 4F-PCC and **IV vitamin K** remains a core treatment.
- For dabigatran, idarucizumab provides specific reversal; confirm whether recent ingestion or renal dysfunction requires reassessment for rebound anticoagulant activity.
- For oral factor-Xa inhibitors, stop the drug and establish last dose, renal function and any anti-Xa assay available, but urgent reversal must not be indefinitely delayed pending an assay when clinically significant drug effect is likely.

- The same 2026 guidance conditionally advises **against platelet transfusion for spontaneous intraparenchymal haemorrhage in antiplatelet-treated patients who are not undergoing neurosurgery**; conversely it supports platelet transfusion in selected aspirin-treated spontaneous ICH patients requiring surgery.
- Evidence for routine desmopressin is uncertain; its use should be described as specialist-dependent rather than obligatory.
- In traumatic intracranial haemorrhage the guideline supports viscoelastic-assay-guided treatment when available; in every setting correction of hypothermia, severe hypocalcaemia and fibrinogen deficiency may matter to haemostasis.

- Distinguish primary haemostatic control from prevention of secondary injury.
- Reversal and blood-pressure treatment cannot evacuate a large extra-axial collection or resolve acute obstructive hydrocephalus.
- Re-examine pupils, GCS, CT mass effect and surgical need continuously, and explicitly discuss the competing **early rebleeding versus later thromboembolic** risks when planning resumption of anticoagulation.

items.title: 6. Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, hydrocephalus and delayed cerebral ischaemia
items.priority: P1 CORE (3 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO) + P5 MINIMUM (2 parent LOs)
items.los: SS_IC 1.83; SS_NS 1.25; AT_RT 1.2; SS_NS 1.6; SS_IC 1.84; SS_NS 1.18
items.body:
## 6.1 The pathophysiological phases explain the management priorities

- Rupture of an intracranial aneurysm causes blood to enter the subarachnoid space and may produce a sudden ICP rise approaching systemic pressure, a transient collapse in cerebral perfusion and global ischaemic injury.
- Patients typically describe an instantaneous **worst-ever or thunderclap headache** with vomiting, photophobia, neck stiffness or collapse; some are initially alert with minimal neurological signs.
- Not every thunderclap headache is SAH, and a negative early CT does not always close the diagnostic pathway: expert evaluation may require lumbar puncture or vascular imaging depending on the time from onset and clinical context.
- Delay is dangerous because an **unsecured aneurysm can rebleed**, often catastrophically.

- The acute priorities are stabilisation without provoking further rupture, reversal of coagulopathy, treatment of hydrocephalus and **early securing of the aneurysm** by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping, ideally within 24 hours at an experienced centre when feasible.
- A clipped or coiled aneurysm is not necessarily the end of the problem.
- Days later, inflammatory and microvascular effects of subarachnoid blood may produce delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI), even without severe angiographic vasospasm.
- The course is complicated by catecholamine surge, cardiac stunning, arrhythmias, neurogenic pulmonary oedema, hyponatraemia and systemic infection.

## 6.2 How to grade severity and what each grade means

- Use both clinical and CT-based systems.
- The **Hunt–Hess scale** broadly ranges from grade I (asymptomatic/minor headache) through II (moderate–severe headache and nuchal rigidity), III (drowsiness/confusion or mild focal deficit), IV (stupor and moderate–severe hemiparesis) to V (deep coma/decerebrate response).

The **WFNS scale** uses GCS and motor deficit:

- Grade I GCS 15 without motor deficit.
- II GCS 13–14 without motor deficit.
- III GCS 13–14 with motor deficit.
- IV GCS 7–12.
- V GCS 3–6.

- Record grades before sedation and note confounders such as seizure or hydrocephalus.
- Prognosis depends on more than a score, and initial severity can improve after CSF drainage or treatment of reversible factors.

**Modified Fisher CT score** estimates the risk associated with blood load and intraventricular haemorrhage:

- Grade 0 no SAH or IVH.
- Grade 1 thin SAH (<1 mm) without IVH.
- Grade 2 thin SAH with IVH.
- Grade 3 thick SAH (≥1 mm) without IVH.
- Grade 4 thick SAH with IVH.

- It is not interchangeable with original Fisher grading.
- Thick cisternal clot and IVH predict DCI/hydrocephalus, but individuals may develop complications at any grade.

## 6.3 Immediate treatment before the aneurysm is secured

- As in all acute brain injury, protect oxygenation, aim for normocapnia, treat pain/nausea/agitation and avoid hypotension.
- A practical pre-securement principle is **smooth BP control without a universal single systolic target**.
- Marked hypertension plausibly increases rebleeding risk, but aggressive BP reduction can compromise perfusion when ICP is high or autoregulation is impaired.
- Many centres use a temporary SBP ceiling around 160 mmHg with nicardipine/labetalol, individualised to pre-morbid BP, neurological state, ICP and neurosurgical advice; the 2023 AHA/ASA guideline does not establish a single outcome-validated BP target in the unsecured aneurysm.
- Avoid wide variability and unnecessary delay.
- Correct anticoagulant effects immediately and treat a seizure if present.

- Acute hydrocephalus is suspected with decreasing consciousness, ventricular enlargement and possible third/fourth ventricle blood.
- EVD placement can rapidly restore consciousness and CPP, but rapid CSF pressure reduction before aneurysm securement can alter transmural aneurysm pressure; neurosurgery prescribes controlled drainage.
- Coiling avoids open craniotomy but needs antithrombotic planning if stent assistance is required; clipping permits direct exclusion and management of selected associated haematomas.
- Discuss with the cerebrovascular team which procedure offers the most durable exclusion for a given aneurysm location, anatomy and patient status.

## 6.4 Nimodipine and pharmacological prevention of delayed cerebral ischaemia

- **Nimodipine** is a lipophilic dihydropyridine L-type calcium-channel antagonist.
- It has an established benefit in reducing poor functional outcome after aneurysmal SAH, commonly given **60 mg enterally every four hours for 21 days**; some patients with hypotension receive 30 mg every two hours according to local protocol.
- Its benefit is not explained simply by reversing large-artery narrowing and probably involves neuroprotective/microcirculatory effects.
- Nimodipine is **enteral, not an IV bolus**; accidentally administering its oral formulation intravenously can be fatal.
- Hypotension is the key treatment-limiting effect; optimise volume and adjust dosing with specialist oversight rather than indiscriminately withholding the drug.

- Other medications have less favourable evidence.
- Routine **statins** or IV **magnesium** to prevent DCI are not recommended.
- Prophylactic vasopressors, hypervolaemia and historical ‘triple-H therapy’ expose patients to pulmonary oedema, cardiac ischaemia and other complications without proven benefit.
- Intrathecal nicardipine, endothelin antagonists, milrinone and other experimental approaches remain centre-specific and should not be represented as universal prophylaxis.
- Short-course antifibrinolytics may be considered only in exceptional unavoidable delays to aneurysm securing under local protocols; routine prolonged tranexamic acid does not improve functional outcomes and may cause harm.

## 6.5 Delayed cerebral ischaemia is not identical to angiographic vasospasm

- DCI typically occurs after aSAH around days **4–14**, with clinical concern through the first two weeks.
- It may appear as new focal weakness, aphasia, declining consciousness or reduced cerebral perfusion after excluding hydrocephalus, rebleeding, seizures, sedation, infection and metabolic causes.
- Large-vessel vasospasm is one mechanism, but cortical spreading depolarisations, microthrombosis, neuroinflammation and microcirculatory dysfunction also contribute.
- Consequently a high TCD velocity is not synonymous with DCI, and normal angiography does not exclude microvascular ischaemia.

- Assess with repeated neurological examinations (sedation minimisation when safe), TCD velocity trends, CTA/CT perfusion and sometimes continuous EEG or invasive monitoring in poor-grade cases.
- A Lindegaard ratio (MCA mean velocity / ipsilateral extracranial ICA velocity) helps distinguish vasospasm from hyperdynamic flow; a ratio >3 supports MCA vasospasm and >6 suggests severe vasospasm, but thresholds are not absolute and other vessels require different interpretation.

### Treatment of symptomatic DCI

- First confirm and exclude other causes, ensure nimodipine is being given, maintain **euvolaemia**, correct hypoxaemia, anaemia and hyponatraemia, and expedite specialist vascular imaging.
- In selected patients with a **secured aneurysm**, a monitored blood-pressure increase with vasopressors (usually noradrenaline) may improve symptoms by increasing collateral flow through narrowed vessels.
- This is **therapeutic hypertension for symptomatic DCI**, not routine prophylactic hypertension; titrate to neurological/perfusion response and monitor the myocardium and lungs.
- If severe or refractory, endovascular balloon angioplasty of accessible proximal spastic arteries or intra-arterial vasodilators (e.g. nicardipine, verapamil, milrinone in specialist practice) may be considered.
- Intra-arterial therapies can cause hypotension and are not guaranteed to prevent infarction.
- Surgical and ICU teams must agree the plan.

## 6.6 Pharmacology and limits of vasospasm treatment

- **Nimodipine prophylaxis** should be understood separately from **endovascular rescue for established vasospasm**.
- Nimodipine is a calcium-channel blocker whose oral use improves functional outcomes after aSAH even though angiographic vasospasm may persist; it is prescribed broadly unless contraindicated.
- By contrast, intra-arterial **nicardipine or verapamil** is delivered by a neurointerventionalist for selected symptomatic narrowing to reduce arterial smooth-muscle tone and improve distal perfusion, potentially at the expense of systemic hypotension or elevated intracranial pressure.
- **Balloon angioplasty** mechanically dilates accessible large proximal vessels and has a more durable anatomical effect in those segments, but cannot safely reach every distal vessel and carries dissection/rupture risk.

- **Milrinone** is a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor that produces arterial vasodilatation and increased cardiac contractility, and some centres use IV or intra-arterial milrinone for refractory DCI/vasospasm.
- However, hypotension, tachyarrhythmias and increased myocardial oxygen demand are relevant hazards, and high-quality outcomes evidence does not yet justify routine adoption for all aSAH.
- **Papaverine** has historical intra-arterial use but neurotoxicity, transient effect and ICP concerns limit enthusiasm.
- An inappropriate shortcut is to give magnesium and statins universally because ‘vasospasm is vascular’; large trials and guideline syntheses do not support such prophylaxis.

- When induced hypertension is chosen, establish what you want to change—**an observable neurological deficit or perfusion abnormality**—and titrate incrementally.
- A poor-grade, intubated patient may not show an obvious limb exam change; CT perfusion, TCD trends, EEG changes or invasive monitoring may help but have limitations.
- Watch for myocardial stunning and pulmonary oedema before escalating noradrenaline; aggressive treatment that improves an angiogram but precipitates severe lung or cardiac injury is not successful management.

## 6.7 Other ICU problems after SAH

- Cardiac troponin rise, QT prolongation, T-wave inversion, arrhythmias and transient LV systolic dysfunction may result from catecholamine-mediated neurocardiac injury.
- Echocardiography is valuable if shock or pulmonary oedema develops; do not assume every troponin elevation is plaque-rupture MI.
- Maintain euvolaemia rather than reflex fluid loading in stunned myocardium.
- Neurogenic pulmonary oedema, aspiration and ventilator-associated infection may coexist.
- Seizure treatment is indicated if seizures occur, commonly for a short period (≈7 days), but **routine anticonvulsant prophylaxis is not recommended for every SAH**; higher-risk patients (MCA aneurysm, cortical infarction, high grade, intraparenchymal bleed or hydrocephalus) warrant individual assessment.
- Phenytoin for routine SAH seizure prevention is associated with excess morbidity and is generally avoided.

Disturbed sodium balance is common and often complicated by fluid loss, hypothalamic injury and endocrine disturbances. **Do not restrict fluid reflexively in SAH-related hyponatraemia:** cerebral salt wasting (CSW) causes renal sodium loss with hypovolaemia, and restricting fluids can worsen DCI. The distinction from SIADH is developed in Chapter 9.

items.title: 7. Prolonged seizures, status epilepticus and perioperative epilepsy
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (1 parent LO) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 7.1 Status epilepticus is a time-dependent medical emergency

- Operationally, **convulsive status epilepticus** is a continuous convulsive seizure lasting **≥5 minutes** or recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness.
- Ongoing seizures become increasingly difficult to terminate as inhibitory GABA-A receptor signalling changes, while excitotoxicity, lactic acidosis, hypoxaemia, rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia and cardiovascular instability accumulate.
- A generalised convulsion lasting more than five minutes therefore deserves immediate benzodiazepine treatment; do not wait the traditional thirty minutes required for some pathological definitions.
- After visible jerking stops, persistent coma may reflect sedatives, brain injury or **nonconvulsive status epilepticus**, requiring EEG rather than reassurance.

- Causes include missed antiepileptic medication, structural stroke/haemorrhage, infection, withdrawal of alcohol/benzodiazepines, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, uraemia, drug toxicity (e.g. tramadol, bupropion, local anaesthetic systemic toxicity), pregnancy-related eclampsia and autoimmune encephalitis.
- Obtain glucose at the bedside, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, gas, temperature, anticonvulsant levels when relevant, infection studies and early imaging as indicated.
- Treat the precipitant while stopping seizures: symptomatic relief alone does not prevent recurrence.

## 7.2 Timed practical treatment sequence

**0–5 minutes:**

- Secure environment, call help, left lateral positioning where feasible, high-flow oxygen when indicated, suction, airway positioning, cardiac/SpO₂/BP monitoring, two IV accesses, check glucose and treat hypoglycaemia.
- Protect from injury, but do not force anything into the mouth or physically restrain a tonic limb.
- If prolonged convulsion, prepare benzodiazepine immediately.

**From five minutes:**

- Give adequate benzodiazepine promptly, not a succession of underdoses.
- Common adult regimens include **lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (usual maximum 4 mg per dose, may repeat once)**; **midazolam 10 mg IM** if IV access is unavailable for adults >40 kg; or IV midazolam according to locally endorsed dosing.
- IV diazepam is an alternative.
- Be ready to ventilate; respiratory depression is less dangerous than ongoing uncontrolled convulsive SE, and both seizures and benzodiazepines can suppress ventilation.

**If seizures continue after adequate benzodiazepine:**

- Give an IV second-line loading agent as soon as feasible: **levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4.5 g)**, **sodium valproate 40 mg/kg (maximum 3 g)**, or **fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (maximum 1.5 g PE)**.
- Where fosphenytoin is unavailable, **phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV** at a suitable maximum administration rate (typically not exceeding 50 mg/min in adults) with ECG/BP monitoring.
- Valproate is undesirable with significant hepatic disease, mitochondrial disease or pregnancy where alternatives exist
- Phenytoin may cause hypotension, dysrhythmia and tissue injury and has interactions
- Levetiracetam is haemodynamically convenient but needs renal maintenance dose adjustment.
- ESETT showed **similar efficacy** for levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate (success around 45–47% at 60 minutes), so the best choice is the one that can be safely and rapidly delivered for that patient.

**Refractory status epilepticus:**

- Persistent seizures despite adequate benzodiazepine and one appropriate second-line medication require ICU, airway protection, continuous EEG and anaesthetic infusion.
- Options include **midazolam** (loading followed by titrated infusion), **propofol** (bolus/infusion with haemodynamic monitoring and vigilance for propofol infusion syndrome), **thiopental/pentobarbital**, or selected **ketamine** (NMDA antagonism) in resistant cases.
- Doses and EEG targets require a local neurocritical protocol; sedation that stops visible movements without electrographic control is not treatment success.
- Continue maintenance antiseizure medications during anaesthetic treatment and investigate autoimmune/infective/metabolic causes.
- Monitor rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, acidosis, aspiration, ARDS and ICU-acquired weakness.

## 7.3 Nonconvulsive status, post-anoxic seizures and EEG

- Nonconvulsive status is clinically subtle: unexplained coma, eyelid twitching, gaze deviation, fluctuation in mental state or merely failure to wake after convulsions may be the only clues.
- Obtain continuous EEG promptly in high-risk cases.
- EEG differentiates ongoing electrographic seizures from postictal encephalopathy, triphasic metabolic patterns and sedative-induced suppression, although interpretation of periodic discharges often requires neurophysiology expertise.
