- Treat definite electrographic status but avoid indiscriminate deep anaesthetic coma for ambiguous patterns without multidisciplinary risk assessment.
- Post-cardiac-arrest seizures and myoclonus require careful evaluation; sedatives and hypoxic injury confound prognosis and isolated myoclonus does not establish irreversibility.

## 7.4 Drug choice in established status epilepticus: an examiner-level comparison

| Antiseizure medicine | Adult loading dose (typical) | Useful attributes | Key limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Levetiracetam | 60 mg/kg IV, max 4.5 g | Minimal hypotension or drug interactions; rapid preparation | Adjust maintenance in renal dysfunction; agitation/behavioural adverse effects |
| Sodium valproate | 40 mg/kg IV, max 3 g | Broad-spectrum efficacy; generally haemodynamically tolerated | Avoid significant liver disease, mitochondrial dysfunction, pregnancy where possible; hyperammonaemia, platelet effects |
| Fosphenytoin | 20 mg PE/kg IV, max 1.5 g PE | Familiar effective option | Hypotension/dysrhythmia, interactions; monitor ECG and pressure; availability varies |
| Phenytoin | 20 mg/kg IV, max 1.5 g | Option if fosphenytoin unavailable | Administration-related cardiac toxicity, extravasation injury and drug interactions |

- Second-line therapy should be a **loading dose**, not a routine daily maintenance dose.
- If a patient has already received a small prophylactic levetiracetam dose, an appropriate loading dose is still needed for SE unless there is a clear pharmacological reason otherwise.
- A delay while seeking an EEG is inappropriate when the patient is obviously convulsing; conversely, persistent depressed consciousness after movement stops justifies urgent EEG.
- Some local protocols use alternative dosing/infusion rates or another first-line benzodiazepine; the principles—rapid adequate treatment, respiratory preparation and cause-directed investigation—are more important than familiarity with a single brand.

- **Refractory SE** management is not simply ‘give more propofol’.
- Clarify the desired EEG endpoint (electrographic seizure suppression, sometimes burst suppression after specialist discussion), duration of seizure control before attempting to wean, maintenance antiepileptic coverage and monitoring for hypotension, acidosis, hypertriglyceridaemia, rhabdomyolysis and propofol infusion syndrome.
- If severe acidosis, renal dysfunction or escalating catecholamine requirements emerge on high-dose propofol, consider toxicity and alternative infusion strategies.
- In children, neonates and pregnancy/eclampsia, distinct protocols apply; in eclampsia **magnesium sulphate**, not the routine adult SE pathway alone, is the disease-specific first-line treatment.

## 7.5 A patient with chronic epilepsy coming for surgery

- Preoperatively identify seizure type, frequency, last event, adherence, triggers, rescue plan, antiepileptic regimen and drug concentrations where indicated.
- Consider underlying lesions and comorbid developmental/neurological disease, aspiration risk, previous status and difficult airway.
- **Continue antiepileptic therapy** perioperatively; give an IV or enteral alternative if the patient cannot take oral medication.

Drug interactions matter:

- Enzyme-inducing agents (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) alter metabolism of some anaesthetics and can produce resistance to nondepolarising neuromuscular blockers.
- Valproate may cause thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction.
- Lamotrigine interacts with some anticonvulsants, and long-term treatment affects bone health and hepatic enzymes.

- During anaesthesia maintain glucose, sodium, oxygen, ventilation and temperature, and avoid missed doses.
- Most routine volatile and IV agents are usable; sevoflurane under some conditions can provoke epileptiform EEG activity, while propofol is anticonvulsant at anaesthetic doses.
- Tramadol lowers seizure threshold, particularly with serotonergic medications, and is usually avoided when alternatives exist.
- An unexpected intraoperative seizure calls for exclusion of local anaesthetic toxicity, hypoglycaemia, hypercarbia/hypoxia and metabolic disturbance, immediate benzodiazepine or propofol, protective airway management, and follow-up neurological assessment.
- Postoperative confusion may be postictal, drug related or an acute neurological event.

## 7.6 Beyond convulsive status: the ICU endpoint and neurological recovery

- The observable end of limb convulsions is not proof that cortical seizures have ceased.
- After adequate benzodiazepine and loading therapy, a patient who remains unexpectedly unconscious, develops subtle ocular movements or receives neuromuscular blockade needs urgent EEG—ideally continuous EEG if ongoing status is suspected.
- The working differential includes nonconvulsive status, postictal suppression, metabolic encephalopathy, encephalitis, acute structural stroke and drug effects.

- Refractory status requires an explicit **EEG target, duration of suppression, maintenance antiseizure plan and weaning schedule** agreed by neurocritical care/neurology.
- Avoid repeating small ineffective sedative boluses that merely conceal motor seizures.
- Continuous infusions may cause hypotension and impair CPP, prolonged ventilation, metabolic complications and propofol-infusion syndrome; concurrent analgesia and paralysis should never be mistaken for antiseizure therapy.
- The exact anaesthetic infusion dose is protocol-specific, but all patients require management of airway, perfusion, glucose, temperature and the cause of seizure recurrence.

- After control, investigate and treat precipitants rather than attributing all status to chronic epilepsy.
- Important causes include missed antiseizure medication, sodium/glucose disturbances, intracranial bleeding, ischaemic stroke, CNS infection, autoimmune encephalitis, toxins and alcohol withdrawal.
- Check for aspiration, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia and renal injury.
- When discussing prognosis distinguish an acute symptomatic seizure, epilepsy, refractory status and post-hypoxic myoclonus; each has a different natural history and treatment threshold.

items.title: 8. Acute spinal cord injury, cord perfusion and autonomic emergencies
items.body:
## 8.1 Mechanisms and clinical localisation

- Acute cord dysfunction can be traumatic (fracture/dislocation, ligament injury, epidural haematoma, penetrating trauma), vascular (anterior spinal ischaemia, aortic surgery, hypotension), compressive (metastasis, abscess, haematoma), inflammatory (myelitis), or metabolic.
- Secondary cord damage arises from ischaemia, oedema, haemorrhage, inflammatory injury, disrupted perfusion and movement of an unstable spine.
- A **high cervical lesion** may immediately threaten ventilation through diaphragm/intercostal dysfunction; a thoracic lesion may spare inspiratory diaphragm function but impair expiratory cough, secretion clearance and abdominal musculature.

- Examine motor and sensory level, spinal tenderness, rectal/sacral function when appropriate, and reflexes.
- The ASIA/ISNCSCI neurological classification distinguishes complete injury (no sacral sparing) from incomplete injury; **sacral sparing** is an important prognostic observation.
- Spinal shock describes transient areflexia/flaccidity below the lesion that evolves over days to spasticity, and is **not the same as neurogenic shock**.
- Conus medullaris or cauda equina compression, with saddle anaesthesia and sphincter dysfunction, requires urgent imaging and specialist assessment.

## 8.2 Initial assessment and immobilisation

- Manage life-threatening haemorrhage and airway threats with **manual in-line stabilisation** when indicated; a rigid collar must not obstruct airway management or jugular venous drainage.
- Use appropriate motion restriction, but do not delay life-saving intubation for perfect radiographs.
- Maintain oxygenation, avoid hypotension and examine neurological function before/after transfer or major interventions.
- CT is first-line for bony injury; MRI defines cord contusion, epidural haematoma, ligamentous disruption and compressive pathology when indicated.
- A normal CT does not exclude cord injury, especially with neurological findings.
- Discuss early decompression/stabilisation, often within 24 hours when feasible; earlier surgery may improve outcomes in selected patients, but urgency also reflects haemodynamics, associated injuries and operative access.

## 8.3 Neurogenic shock and targeted spinal cord perfusion

- A lesion above the thoracolumbar sympathetic outflow can remove sympathetic tone, causing **hypotension, peripheral vasodilatation and sometimes bradycardia**, particularly with high cervical or upper thoracic injury.
- This is neurogenic shock and must not be diagnosed until haemorrhage, tension pneumothorax and cardiac injury have been considered.
- Tachycardia does not reliably exclude cord injury, but an unexpectedly low heart rate during profound hypotension raises suspicion.
- Treat initial haemorrhage with appropriate blood products; for persistent neurogenic vasoplegia use judicious isotonic fluid to correct true deficit and **noradrenaline** to restore vascular tone while supporting cardiac output.
- High spinal injuries can cause severe bradycardia/asystole with airway stimulation; have atropine and resuscitation equipment available and consider pacing for refractory episodes.

- The **2024 acute SCI haemodynamic guideline** suggests a MAP **lower limit 75–80 mmHg**, without actively pushing above an **upper limit 90–95 mmHg**, for **3–7 days**.
- These are weak recommendations based on very-low-quality evidence, replacing simplistic mandatory MAP >85 mmHg for everyone.
- The practical message is to avoid hypotension and individualise pressor targets based on cardiac tolerance, neurological trajectory and injury.
- The guideline could not recommend a single preferred vasopressor or invasive SCPP target.
- Monitor arrhythmias, myocardial ischaemia, fluid overload and tissue injury from vasoconstriction; use an arterial line and ICU observation for significant high lesions.

## 8.4 Distinguish the cord emergencies by lesion and physiology

| Pattern | Typical findings | Most urgent danger |
|---|---|---|
| High cervical complete injury | Quadriplegia, impaired diaphragm/intercostals, autonomic instability | Respiratory collapse, bradycardia, shock |
| Anterior spinal artery syndrome | Motor and pain-temperature loss, relatively spared vibration/position | Ischaemic cord infarction; hypotension or vascular cause |
| Central cord syndrome | Arms often weaker than legs; variable bladder dysfunction | Occult cervical stenosis/trauma with progressive deficit |
| Brown–Séquard syndrome | Ipsilateral weakness/position loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss | Hemicord lesion requiring imaging and stabilisation |
| Cauda equina compression | Saddle anaesthesia, radicular pain, sphincter dysfunction, lower motor neuron signs | Time-critical decompression of compressive pathology |
| Epidural haematoma/abscess | New severe spinal pain, focal motor/sensory deficit, fever sometimes absent | Immediate MRI, neurosurgical decompression and cause-directed treatment |

- In a trauma patient with severe hypotension after cervical SCI, the distinction between **haemorrhagic shock** and **neurogenic shock** is crucial.
- Both can coexist: a warm, bradycardic patient may still have abdominal or pelvic bleeding.
- Use eFAST/CT and haemorrhage assessment, not just pulse rate, to exclude blood loss.
- Initial vasopressor use without replacing haemorrhage would worsen oxygen delivery, but repeated unnecessary litres of crystalloid in pure vasoplegia can cause pulmonary oedema and impair ventilatory function.
- Titrate blood products, crystalloid and noradrenaline to the actual physiology.

- **Spinal cord protection during vascular interventions** follows the same MAP–CSF pressure framework but may require a different specialist bundle: preservation of haemoglobin and cardiac output, avoidance of prolonged aortic hypotension, reimplantation/preservation of segmental supply where feasible, and in selected high-risk thoracoabdominal aortic procedures a lumbar CSF drain under carefully controlled pressure and coagulation precautions.
- Drain complications include intracranial/subdural bleeding, infection and spinal haematoma; the drain is not benign.
- This overlaps with the later vascular teaching set, but the perfusion physiology belongs here.

## 8.5 Anaesthesia and intensive care for acute SCI

- Prepare for difficult airway due to collar, swelling, facial trauma or urgent instability.
- Video laryngoscopy with competent manual in-line stabilisation is often useful; awake intubation is an option when a cooperative patient and a high-risk unstable spine warrant it, but may be impossible in injured or hypoxaemic patients.
- Avoid succinylcholine after the period when denervation-related extrajunctional acetylcholine receptor proliferation becomes clinically relevant (often from **48 hours after major denervating injury** onward) because of life-threatening hyperkalaemia; the exact onset varies with injury severity and evolution.
- Nondepolarising agents with appropriate monitoring and reversal are preferred after this period.

- Ventilatory failure can evolve over the first days as oedema progresses; assess vital capacity, cough peak flow, secretion burden, ABG and serial respiratory fatigue.
- Bronchial hygiene, assisted cough, appropriate humidification, early tracheostomy in selected patients and pneumonia prevention are important.
- Gastric ileus, bladder dysfunction, pressure injury, DVT/PE, neuropathic pain, dysreflexia and temperature dysregulation require active prevention.
- Rehabilitation and coordinated psychosocial support start early.
- **High-dose methylprednisolone is not routine standard care** after SCI because evidence for meaningful benefit is uncertain and infection/GI bleeding risks are substantial.

## 8.6 Chronic cord injury: autonomic dysreflexia, spinal physiology and surgery

- **Autonomic dysreflexia (AD)** typically occurs in chronic lesions at/above **T6**, after spinal shock resolves.
- Noxious input below the lesion (bladder distension, blocked catheter, bowel impaction, pressure or surgical stimuli) causes uncontrolled sympathetic discharge with profound hypertension, headache, flushing/sweating above lesion, pallor below and reflex bradycardia.
- The patient may perceive little pain despite life-threatening BP.
- Immediate management is to sit the patient upright (unless contraindicated), stop the stimulus, loosen constricting garments, check drainage/catheter and bowel/skin causes, monitor BP frequently, and give a short-acting antihypertensive (e.g. nitrates or carefully titrated IV agent) if severe or persistent.
- Avoid provoking sudden rebound hypotension when the trigger is removed.

- Before anaesthesia document injury level, baseline BP (often low), airway/respiratory function, sleep apnoea, scoliosis, prior AD, urinary devices, skin condition and VTE risk.
- Neuraxial anaesthesia can suppress AD if block height is adequate; general anaesthesia requires sufficient depth/analgesia and ready antihypertensives.
- High cervical lesions may have impaired thermoregulation and exaggerated responses to positive-pressure ventilation.
- Chronic immobilisation can lead to joint contractures, positioning injury, osteoporosis and fragility fractures.
- Distinguish the autonomic dysreflexia of a chronic cord lesion from the **neurogenic shock** of an acute lesion.

## 8.7 Acute and chronic spinal cord complications beyond blood-pressure targets

- Spinal cord injury severity should be documented with **ISNCSCI/ASIA** motor and sensory examination when clinically feasible, including the neurological level and sacral sparing.
- A clinically complete injury is not identical to a radiologically transected cord.
- Distinguish **spinal shock** (temporary flaccidity/areflexia below injury), **neurogenic shock** (loss of sympathetic tone causing hypotension and often bradycardia, usually high thoracic/cervical lesions) and **autonomic dysreflexia** (later episodic hypertension from noxious stimuli below a typically T6-or-above lesion).
- These syndromes have different haemodynamic treatments.

- Respiratory impairment depends strongly on neurological level: C3–5 phrenic motor supply and high cervical injuries threaten diaphragmatic ventilation; lower cervical and thoracic injuries cause weak intercostal/abdominal muscles, ineffective cough and secretion retention.
- Serial vital capacity and cough strength, gas exchange and aspiration risk are more informative than a single pulse oximeter reading.
- Plan airway and ventilation with full spine precautions and minimise secondary cord injury from hypoxaemia or hypotension.

- Acute neurological deterioration is not always traumatic contusion.
- Consider **epidural haematoma**, abscess, malignant spinal cord compression, disc extrusion, vascular malformation, spinal infarction after aortic procedures and inflammatory transverse myelitis.
- A painful, progressive compressive deficit warrants urgent MRI and spinal/neurosurgical review; in cancer-associated compression, dexamethasone and definitive decompression/radiotherapy are specialist-directed and should not be delayed by a generic traumatic-SCI pathway.
- In aortic surgery, spinal cord perfusion may depend on distal arterial pressure and CSF pressure; rescue can involve optimising MAP/haemoglobin and CSF drainage under a formal vascular protocol.

- Long-term care includes DVT prophylaxis, bowel and bladder programmes, pressure prevention, neuropathic pain, spasticity, infection surveillance and rehabilitation.
- For chronic high lesions, identify past autonomic dysreflexia, trigger patterns (especially bladder instrumentation), baseline BP and any autonomic medication before anaesthesia.
- Management begins with stopping the trigger and bladder decompression, then short-acting BP control if needed.
- Observe for recurrent hypotension after stimulus removal.

items.title: 9. The neurosurgical ICU: sodium disorders, postoperative care and long-term impairment
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P2 HIGH (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 9.1 Why sodium disturbances are common after cranial injury or surgery

- Hypothalamic/pituitary dysfunction, cerebral inflammation, natriuretic peptide release, non-osmotic antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin) secretion, fluid administration and renal injury make sodium and water balance unstable after SAH, TBI and pituitary/neurosurgical procedures.
- Sodium matters because it determines plasma tonicity and thus transcellular water movement: a rapid fall in extracellular sodium can cause **cerebral oedema**; excessively rapid correction of established chronic hyponatraemia can cause **osmotic demyelination syndrome**.
- Hypernatraemia raises extracellular tonicity and draws water out of brain cells; rapid correction of longstanding hypernatraemia can cause cerebral oedema.
- Symptoms and urgency depend on absolute concentration, rate of change and brain pathology, not the number alone.

- Begin by checking measured serum sodium, plasma osmolality, glucose (correct sodium interpretation for hyperglycaemia), urine osmolality, urine sodium and potassium, renal function, and **actual volume status**.
- Hourly urine output, daily cumulative balance, serial body weight, BP, haematocrit and bedside echocardiography can help.
- Serum sodium is a concentration, so it changes with both total sodium and total body water.
- Large volumes of electrolyte-free water administered to a patient with inappropriate antidiuresis can rapidly worsen hyponatraemia.

## 9.2 SIADH versus cerebral salt wasting (CSW)

| Feature | SIADH | Cerebral salt wasting / renal salt wasting |
|---|---|---|
| Primary mechanism | ADH effect causes inappropriate water retention | Renal sodium loss leads to extracellular volume depletion, often after brain injury |
| Serum sodium and osmolality | Low sodium, hypotonic plasma | Low sodium, hypotonic plasma |
| Urine | Inappropriately concentrated, often urinary sodium >30 mmol/L | Concentrated with often high urine sodium; volume of urine may be high |
| Clinical extracellular volume | Usually euvolaemic on clinical assessment | **Hypovolaemic**: negative balance, weight loss, hypotension/tachycardia, rising urea/haematocrit where present |
| Main management | Treat cause; fluid restriction for suitable stable patients, sometimes hypertonic saline if symptomatic | Replace water and sodium losses with isotonic/hypertonic saline; consider fludrocortisone in selected cases |
| Why the distinction matters in SAH | Excess fluid can worsen hyponatraemia | Fluid restriction can worsen intravascular depletion and cerebral ischaemia |

- Clinical volume assessment is imperfect, and ADH levels are not a routine differentiating test.
- Fractional excretion of urate may remain raised after correction in renal salt wasting but often normalises with corrected SIADH, although it is not a stand-alone validated test in every ICU patient.
- Exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and diuretics, which can mimic both syndromes.
- **Do not label any SAH patient with hyponatraemia ‘SIADH’ automatically.** Because euvolaemia is critical for preventing DCI, significant natriuresis and negative fluid balance usually require replacement while the diagnosis is clarified.

## 9.3 Treatment of symptomatic hyponatraemia

- Severe symptoms such as seizures, coma, marked confusion or signs of herniation require urgent hypertonic saline **regardless of the ultimate cause**.
- One widely used regimen is **3% NaCl 100–150 mL IV over 10–20 minutes**, with repeat boluses guided by symptoms and sodium response (local protocols vary).
- An early rise around **4–6 mmol/L** is often sufficient to arrest hyponatraemic seizures and reduce cerebral swelling; do not aim to normalise sodium in the first hour.
- Recheck sodium after boluses and regularly (often every 2–4 h during active correction), monitor urine output, and avoid overcorrection once the underlying stimulus reverses and brisk water diuresis begins.

- For chronic or unknown-duration hyponatraemia, commonly used general safety limits are **no more than 8 mmol/L in 24 h** in patients at high risk of osmotic demyelination (e.g. malnutrition, alcoholism, hypokalaemia, severe chronic low sodium, liver disease), with individual specialist targets.
- Some protocols allow up to 10 mmol/L initially in lower-risk patients, but the safer approach is to aim conservatively and check frequently.
- If sodium is rising unexpectedly rapidly, stop inappropriate saline and consider **desmopressin plus electrolyte-free water** under specialist supervision to prevent or reverse overcorrection.
- Treat hypokalaemia carefully: potassium replacement itself can raise serum sodium/effective tonicity.

- For CSW, replace actual urinary fluid and salt losses, often with isotonic saline plus additional sodium or hypertonic saline if needed.
- **Fludrocortisone** (for example 0.1 mg daily or twice daily, adjusted to response) can reduce natriuresis in selected SAH patients, but monitor hypokalaemia, hypertension and fluid overload.
- For SIADH, choose treatment by symptoms, severity and fluid needs; conventional fluid restriction may be inappropriate during active SAH when cerebral perfusion is threatened.
- Vasopressin antagonists can produce rapid unpredictable correction and are not a routine first-line neuro-ICU treatment.

## 9.4 Diabetes insipidus and postoperative hypernatraemia

- Central **arginine vasopressin deficiency** (formerly central diabetes insipidus, DI) may follow pituitary/hypothalamic surgery, severe TBI or brain death.
- Deficient ADH causes high-volume dilute urine, hypernatraemia and increasing plasma osmolality when water cannot be replaced.
- Consider it with urine output often >200–300 mL/h for several hours, urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg or very low specific gravity, and rising serum sodium; osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia, mannitol, high urea load or diuretics must be excluded.
- In partial DI the urine may not be maximally dilute.
- **Post-pituitary surgery may show a triphasic response:** early DI, transient SIADH from release of stored hormone, then potentially permanent DI if neuronal injury is substantial.

- Treat by restoring circulation and replacing estimated water deficit plus continuing losses, preferentially enterally if safe or with controlled IV free water (e.g. 5% dextrose) as appropriate.
- **Desmopressin** (DDAVP) is used for central deficiency, with small IV/subcutaneous doses (e.g. 0.5–2 micrograms) or an oral/intranasal formulation depending on acuity; titrate against urine output, osmolality and sodium.
- Do not administer repeated desmopressin without monitoring because water retention can rapidly cause hyponatraemia once fluid access resumes.
- For chronic hypernatraemia aim for cautious correction, often no faster than approximately 0.5 mmol/L/h with an individual daily plan; true acute hypernatraemia may be corrected more rapidly in specialist settings, balancing cerebral swelling and ongoing water loss.

## 9.5 Systematic care after neurosurgery

- The first postoperative hour establishes a **new neurological baseline**.
- Handover must include preoperative deficit, operation, expected complications, blood loss and anticoagulants, intraoperative BP/ventilation incidents, drugs likely to delay awakening, drains/EVD instructions, sodium targets and rescue thresholds.
- Frequent GCS component and pupil examinations detect haematoma, hydrocephalus, stroke and seizures.
- A new severe headache, agitation, vomiting, aphasia, hemiparesis or declining consciousness after craniotomy is a complication until proved otherwise.
- Check haemodynamics, glucose, ABG and sodium, secure oxygenation, liaise urgently and obtain imaging as needed.

- Post-craniotomy pain is often substantial despite historic beliefs to the contrary.
- Inadequate treatment causes sympathetic hypertension, coughing, agitation and vomiting—each potentially raising ICP and obscuring the neurological examination.
- Use **multimodal analgesia** with regular paracetamol, judicious titrated opioid and, where appropriate, scalp infiltration or regional scalp blocks; consider NSAIDs only with attention to bleeding, renal function and the neurosurgeon’s assessment.
- The **2025 Australasian Anaesthesia Blue Book chapter, ‘Post-craniotomy pain: Analgesia and scalp blocks’** reviews the evidence that scalp blocks reduce acute pain and opioid requirements.
- Avoid oversedation, hypotension and severe nausea; prophylactic antiemetics are valuable.
- Keep the head elevated when appropriate, the neck neutral, and protect venous drainage.

- A typical craniotomy ICU plan also addresses early extubation when safe, residual weakness, seizures, temperature, infection, wound/CSF leak, VTE prophylaxis timing, corticosteroid plans for tumour oedema where indicated (note: **not** routine TBI therapy), endocrine sequelae of pituitary surgery, electrolytes, nutrition and functional rehabilitation.
- EVD systems require dedicated nursing competence and clear drainage/monitoring orders.
- Deterioration after clipping/coiling also requires assessment for rebleeding, vasospasm/DCI and hydrocephalus.

## 9.6 Hemiplegia, paraplegia, quadriplegia and rehabilitation

- Long-term neurological deficits create persistent risks: dysphagia and aspiration after stroke, immobility-associated VTE, pressure injury, contractures, bowel/bladder dysfunction, pneumonia, neuropathic pain, depression and loss of function.
- A person with quadriplegia may have respiratory muscle weakness, ineffective cough, autonomic dysfunction, difficult positioning and thermoregulatory problems even when otherwise medically stable.
- Daily care therefore includes safe positioning, assisted secretion clearance, early graded mobilisation and rehabilitation, swallow assessment and nutritional planning, bowel/bladder programmes and prevention of skin breakdown.
- Goals of care should be based on patient values and evolving functional recovery, not an isolated score during sedative exposure.

## 9.7 A complication-oriented postoperative neurosurgical surveillance plan

- Post-craniotomy and pituitary patients can deteriorate through **bleeding, acute hydrocephalus, cerebral oedema, seizures, pneumocephalus, ischaemia, vasospasm, CSF leak and meningitis**.
- A safe postoperative plan therefore specifies the expected neurological baseline, frequency of pupils/GCS/focal motor assessments, blood-pressure ceiling or CPP floor, drains/EVD levels, sodium-fluid strategy, antiepileptic treatment and the escalation criteria that trigger repeat imaging.
- An uneventful operation is not evidence that these complications have been excluded.

**Early unexpected failure to wake:**

- Review drugs and quantitative NMBA recovery, but examine pupils and motor asymmetry before assuming sedation.
- Urgent CT assesses new haemorrhage, hydrocephalus, mass effect and pneumocephalus; CTA/vascular imaging is needed if infarction or vascular injury is suspected.
- Persistent focal deficit or seizures may require MRI/EEG.
- If a patient has an EVD, the prescribed height, position and clamp policy are part of the handover.
- Opening a drain or changing the patient’s position without re-levelling can produce overdrainage, inaccurate pressure measurement or new haemorrhage.

- **After transsphenoidal surgery**, record hourly urine output and regular serum sodium/osmolality; distinguish central DI from osmotic diuresis or excess fluid.
- Marked hypotonic polyuria with rising serum sodium usually suggests DI and requires measured replacement plus titrated desmopressin.
- Hyponatraemia several days later may represent SIADH; a triphasic response can follow stalk injury.
- After SAH, true hypovolaemia with renal sodium loss argues for cerebral salt wasting rather than simple water restriction.
- Sodium correction must also account for seizures, cerebral oedema and risk of osmotic demyelination from overrapid chronic hyponatraemia correction.

**Analgesia and recovery:**

- Provide multimodal analgesia and antiemetics while preserving the ability to conduct a useful neurological examination.
- Consider local infiltration or scalp block where appropriate; avoid treating pain-related hypertension with excessive anaesthetic deepening that conceals deterioration.
- Swallow evaluation, safe mobilisation, VTE prevention after stable postoperative imaging, nutrition and early physiotherapy address disability and pulmonary complications.
- Dexamethasone may be indicated for vasogenic oedema from selected tumours, but is **not** routine treatment for traumatic brain injury.

items.title: 10. Neuromuscular disease and the perioperative anaesthetist
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P2 HIGH (1 parent LO) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 10.1 A localisation approach avoids memorising unrelated diseases

- Weakness can arise from anterior horn cell, peripheral nerve, neuromuscular junction or muscle.
- The lesion predicts the perioperative hazard.
- **Peripheral neuropathies** produce denervation and may cause respiratory muscle weakness plus autonomic instability
- **junction disorders** (myasthenia) impair transmission and show characteristic drug sensitivity
- **muscle disease** (dystrophies, myotonia) can cause cardiomyopathy, respiratory restriction, rhabdomyolysis and exaggerated potassium release with depolarising blockers.
- Central disorders such as Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis and cerebral palsy add aspiration, positioning and medication-continuity problems.
- Across all, the most important preoperative questions are bulbar function, cough, orthopnoea, nocturnal hypoventilation, respiratory infections, ventilatory support, cardiac involvement and previous anaesthetic complications.

- Respiratory evaluation should not rely on resting SpO₂ alone.
- Neuromuscular hypoventilation initially causes nocturnal CO₂ retention while oxygen saturation may look acceptable awake.
- Assess upright/supine vital capacity, cough strength or peak cough flow, inspiratory pressure (NIF/MIP), capnography or arterial/venous blood gas when indicated, and need for NIV.
- Dropping supine VC suggests diaphragm weakness.
- Feeding/swallowing and secretion management are as important as intubation difficulty.
- Document baseline limb/cranial weakness to distinguish postoperative disease progression from residual neuromuscular blockade.

## 10.2 Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS): peripheral nerve inflammation and respiratory failure

- GBS is an acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy, often following gastrointestinal or respiratory infection (including Campylobacter).
- The common acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy subtype causes progressive, often symmetrical ascending weakness, areflexia and paraesthesias; acute motor axonal forms and Miller Fisher syndrome (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia) also occur.
- Nerve conduction studies and CSF (albuminocytological dissociation) support diagnosis but may be normal early.
- Rapid progression, bulbar weakness, respiratory dysfunction and autonomic instability demand ICU assessment even before profound ventilatory failure.

- Respiratory risk is assessed by **serial** clinical examination and mechanics.
- Warning signs include rapidly progressive weakness, weak cough, inability to lift head, dysphagia/dysarthria, tachypnoea, declining VC and impaired inspiratory pressure.
- The traditional **20/30/40** warning framework (VC <20 mL/kg, NIF magnitude <30 cmH₂O, or maximal expiratory pressure <40 cmH₂O) helps identify risk but is not a standalone intubation rule.
- Intubate before exhaustion or aspiration if trajectory is poor.
- Bulbar dysfunction makes NIV risky in some patients.
- Autonomic episodes produce labile BP, tachyarrhythmias or severe bradycardia/asystole; use invasive monitoring when severe and have treatment ready for suction-induced bradycardia.

- Definitive disease-modifying treatment is **IV immunoglobulin** (commonly 0.4 g/kg/day for five days) **or plasma exchange** (typically several exchanges over 1–2 weeks), selected by neurologist and patient factors.
- Corticosteroids alone do not provide an established recovery benefit in typical GBS.
- Prevent DVT, infection, pressure injury, pain and contractures; recovery may take months and neuropathic pain is common.
- Succinylcholine is contraindicated during active denervation and recovery because of severe hyperkalaemia risk, sometimes long after apparent strength improves.
- Nondepolarising relaxants can have prolonged and unpredictable action, so minimise doses, use quantitative monitoring and plan ventilatory recovery.
- Prolonged weakness is not always due to residual relaxant: disease progression and ICU-acquired weakness must be considered.

## 10.3 Myasthenia gravis (MG): physiology predicts drug sensitivity

- MG is usually an antibody-mediated disorder of the **postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor** (AChR) or associated neuromuscular-junction proteins (e.g. MuSK), reducing the safety factor for neuromuscular transmission.
- Fatigable ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia and proximal limb weakness vary during the day and with exertion; respiratory muscle involvement can cause myasthenic crisis.
- Ask about bulbar symptoms, prior crisis/intubation, thymoma, recent infection and medication changes, and establish disease severity and baseline respiratory reserve.
- Antibody tests, repetitive nerve stimulation/single-fibre EMG and clinical neurology assessment establish disease subtype.
- **MuSK-associated MG often has more prominent bulbar involvement**, influencing airway risk.

- **Pyridostigmine** inhibits acetylcholinesterase and improves transmission; continue perioperatively where feasible, with an alternative route plan if NPO for long periods.
- Some patients take corticosteroids or steroid-sparing immunosuppression; consider infection risk and the need for perioperative stress-dose glucocorticoids according to adrenal suppression risk.
- Elective surgery is best performed during stable disease with a plan agreed by neurology, anaesthesia and surgery.
- The **BJA Education 2021 review by Daum, Smelt and Ibrahim** is particularly useful here because it explicitly develops preoperative optimisation, muscle relaxant handling and crisis differentiation.

- MG patients are **sensitive to nondepolarising neuromuscular blockers**, sometimes dramatically; if paralysis is necessary, give carefully titrated small doses of rocuronium under **quantitative** monitoring and consider sugammadex reversal while recognising occasional incomplete recovery.
- Avoid NMBA where appropriate, but inadequate anaesthesia and poorly controlled airway conditions are not safer.
- Responses to succinylcholine are variable and may be resistant due to reduced receptor number, while pyridostigmine may prolong its breakdown; it is often avoided in favour of a controllable plan.
- Neostigmine reversal can be unpredictable in patients already receiving anticholinesterases; if excessive it may contribute to cholinergic manifestations.
- Check quantitative TOF ratio ≥0.9 and clinical strength before extubation, and be conservative when bulbar/respiratory function is compromised.

- **Myasthenic crisis** is respiratory/bulbar failure from under-treatment, infection, surgery or medication-triggered exacerbation.
- **Cholinergic crisis** results from excess acetylcholinesterase inhibition and may feature marked muscarinic signs (salivation, lacrimation, diarrhoea, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia, miosis) along with weakness; it is rarer in modern care.
- At the bedside, the distinction cannot be made simply by weakness alone.
- Protect the airway, ventilate if needed, involve neurology, identify triggers and use IVIG or plasma exchange for significant myasthenic crisis; adjust anticholinesterase therapy under specialist guidance.
- Magnesium, aminoglycosides, some fluoroquinolones/macrolides, beta-blockers and other medications may worsen junctional weakness: weigh risk and select alternatives when reasonable.

## 10.4 Myasthenic versus Lambert–Eaton syndromes

- Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome involves **presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies**, often paraneoplastic (especially small-cell lung carcinoma).
- Proximal leg weakness, hyporeflexia, autonomic symptoms (dry mouth) and facilitation of strength after repeated contraction distinguish it from many MG presentations.
- It may cause marked sensitivity to neuromuscular blockers and autonomic instability.
- The treatment of the underlying tumour and agents such as amifampridine are relevant; preoperative respiratory and bulbar assessment remains important.
- Do not assume a standard ‘MG’ NMBA regimen is safe in Lambert–Eaton syndrome.

## 10.5 Muscular dystrophies, inflammatory myopathy and myotonic disorders

- In **Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy**, dystrophin deficiency causes membrane fragility and progressive skeletal and cardiac myopathy.
- DMD patients often have restrictive respiratory weakness, obstructive sleep apnoea, scoliosis and dilated cardiomyopathy or conduction disease.
- Volatile agents and succinylcholine can trigger **anaesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalaemic arrest**, which is not the same genetic mechanism as classic malignant hyperthermia.
- For DMD, a **trigger-free TIVA technique with nondepolarising relaxation if necessary** is generally preferred, with active cardiac/respiratory preparation and postoperative ventilation planning.
- Suxamethonium is contraindicated.
- Avoid large fluid loads in cardiomyopathy; ECG and echocardiography are essential according to severity.

- In **myotonic dystrophy**, delayed relaxation after contraction (myotonia) may be provoked by cold, shivering, mechanical stimulation or electrical stimulation.
- Associated conduction disease, arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, respiratory weakness, sleep-disordered breathing, gastrointestinal dysmotility and aspiration risk may dominate perioperative outcomes.
- Sensitivity to sedatives/opioids can be profound; use cautious doses and objective recovery monitoring.
- Succinylcholine can precipitate severe contraction and a difficult airway; neostigmine may aggravate myotonia and should be approached cautiously.
- Prevention of hypothermia and shivering is particularly important.
- Evaluate pacemaker/ICD history where relevant.

- **Inflammatory myopathies** such as polymyositis or dermatomyositis can cause proximal weakness, interstitial lung disease, dysphagia/aspiration and myocarditis.
- Steroid therapy may suppress the adrenal axis.
- **Mitochondrial myopathies** can impair oxidative metabolism, producing lactic acidosis, poor fasting tolerance and variable anaesthetic sensitivity; avoid unnecessary prolonged fasting and tailor propofol exposure when concerned about mitochondrial dysfunction.
- Distinguish primary myopathy from neuropathy through CK, distribution of weakness, EMG and specialist testing, not only the word ‘muscle weakness’.

## 10.6 Multiple sclerosis (MS)

- MS is an immune-mediated CNS demyelinating condition with focal relapsing deficits or progressive disability.
- Preoperative assessment focuses on current relapse, baseline motor/sensory state, autonomic/bladder dysfunction, respiratory involvement when advanced, disease-modifying therapy (infection/immunosuppression risks), spasticity and temperature sensitivity.
- A small increase in body temperature may worsen conduction through previously demyelinated pathways (**Uhthoff phenomenon**) without implying a new inflammatory relapse.
- Maintain normothermia and avoid infection, severe stress and prolonged physiological disturbances.

- Neither general anaesthesia nor neuraxial techniques are categorically contraindicated solely because of MS; select according to surgical needs, neurological status, anticoagulation and shared discussion.
- Document baseline findings to interpret postoperative symptoms.
- Spinal anaesthesia has historically raised concern about exposure of demyelinated neural tissue to local anaesthetic, but high-quality evidence of universal harm is lacking.
- Epidural techniques may be reasonable with judicious dosing.
- Avoid succinylcholine in patients with major upper motor neuron injury and denervation/immobility because hyperkalaemia is possible.
- Baclofen withdrawal may cause severe spasticity, fever or rhabdomyolysis, especially with an intrathecal pump; confirm pump function and medication continuity.

## 10.7 Parkinson disease

- Parkinson disease is a progressive central dopaminergic disorder producing bradykinesia, rigidity, rest tremor, gait difficulty and variable autonomic/psychiatric symptoms.
- Severe dysphagia, delayed gastric emptying, aspiration, orthostatic hypotension, depression, delirium and cognitive impairment are common perioperative concerns.
- **Do not abruptly omit levodopa/carbidopa:** missed doses cause rigidity, immobility, respiratory compromise and, rarely, a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome with hyperpyrexia and autonomic instability.
- Arrange exact medication timing and an enteral or specialist alternative when oral swallowing is impossible.

- Avoid centrally acting dopamine-antagonist antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, droperidol) where feasible because they can worsen parkinsonism; ondansetron is commonly suitable, but review serotonergic interactions in patients taking MAO-B inhibitors (e.g. selegiline or rasagiline).
- Certain opioids, particularly pethidine/meperidine or tramadol, pose serotonergic risk with MAO inhibitors.
- Treat orthostatic hypotension and aspiration risk.
- Deep brain stimulators require planning for electrosurgery/diathermy, device interrogation, possible shutdown and postoperative reactivation, with clear documentation and device-team advice.

## 10.8 Cerebral palsy (CP)

- CP is a nonprogressive brain lesion producing lifelong motor/postural impairment, but the secondary musculoskeletal, respiratory, nutritional and pain complications may evolve.
- Assess the patient’s usual communication method, developmental/cognitive profile, seizures, scoliosis/restrictive physiology, gastro-oesophageal reflux, drooling, dysphagia, aspiration history, contractures, osteoporosis, nutritional status and prior airway experience.
- A patient may understand complex discussions despite severe dysarthria; speak directly to them and include supporters appropriately.
- Difficult positioning, IV access and hypothermia are common; autonomic or drug-related temperature dysregulation may coexist.

- Medication reconciliation includes antiepileptics, antispasticity agents (baclofen), benzodiazepines, anticholinergics and botulinum toxin programmes.
- Do not interrupt baclofen or anticonvulsant regimens without a plan.
- Increased oropharyngeal secretions and reflux may justify a protected airway and careful aspiration precautions.
- Neuromuscular blocking requirements can vary with muscle mass, anticonvulsant use and prior neurological injury; use quantitative monitoring rather than relying on simple textbook assumptions.
- Postoperative pain assessment must adapt to nonverbal communication and individual baseline behaviours.
- The **BJA Education 2022 ‘Anaesthesia and cerebral palsy’** review is a useful direct reference.

## 10.9 Neuromuscular blockade in critical illness and ICU-acquired weakness

- A paralysed critically ill patient cannot signal awareness, pain or dyspnoea.
- Reserve prolonged NMBA infusions for clear indications (e.g. selected severe ARDS with ventilator dyssynchrony, life-threatening ICP crises or difficult therapeutic procedures), and reassess daily.
- Provide **reliable sedation and analgesia before** paralysis, as well as eye lubrication, pressure protection, thromboprophylaxis and neuromuscular monitoring where technically feasible.
- Paralysis obscures seizures and clinical neurological deterioration, increasing the need for EEG and alternative monitoring.
- Prolonged blockade is more likely with organ dysfunction, electrolyte/acid–base changes, hypothermia, drug accumulation and altered neuromuscular physiology.

- **ICU-acquired weakness** can arise from critical illness polyneuropathy (axonal sensorimotor neuropathy), critical illness myopathy (myosin loss and muscle dysfunction) or both.
- Sepsis, multiorgan failure, immobility and hyperglycaemia are prominent risk factors; associations with corticosteroids or NMBAs vary by setting and do not mean that one brief exposure invariably causes the condition.
- Symmetrical limb weakness, depressed reflexes, difficulty weaning and preserved facial/ocular function favour ICU-acquired weakness, whereas new focal deficits require a stroke/spinal evaluation.
- Use clinical examination, nerve conduction studies/EMG when needed and a rehabilitation/weaning plan.
- **Do not confuse failure to move under sedation/paralysis with neurological death.**

## 10.10 Evaluating neuromuscular blockade in critical illness (SS_IC 1.7)

- A neuromuscular blocking agent (NMBA) suppresses muscle activity; it provides **no amnesia, hypnosis, analgesia or seizure suppression**.
- Before a continuous infusion, explicitly document the indication, expected physiological benefit, alternatives, sedation/analgesia plan, review time and monitoring.
- Short-term indications include intubation, severe ventilator dyssynchrony preventing lung-protective ventilation, selected severe ARDS with persistent hypoxaemia, procedures or rescue of dangerous ICP surges driven by coughing/movement.
- Routine prolonged paralysis simply to make ventilation easier exposes the patient to avoidable harms.

- The **2026 SCCM ARDS guideline** conditionally suggests NMBA use in ARDS with **PaO₂/FiO₂ <150** when patients remain hypoxaemic or cannot achieve ventilation targets despite optimisation of sedation and ventilator settings.
- If used, limit duration and do **not routinely exceed 48 hours**.
- This recommendation does not mean every patient with P/F <150 should be paralysed, or that all prone patients require paralysis.
- The earlier ACURASYS trial suggested benefit with early cisatracurium in selected severe ARDS, whereas ROSE did not show a survival advantage for routine early continuous blockade compared with lighter-sedation usual care.
- Differences in cointerventions and sedation prevent simplistic trial equivalence.

**Drug choice depends on organ function and haemodynamics:**

- Cisatracurium and atracurium undergo substantial organ-independent breakdown via Hofmann elimination (atracurium additionally ester hydrolysis), making them useful in renal/hepatic impairment; atracurium can release histamine.
- Rocuronium and vecuronium may accumulate in hepatic disease/renal dysfunction, depending on agent and metabolites.
- Aminosteroid agents can sometimes be antagonised with sugammadex when appropriate, but the need for reliable extubation and major renal impairment influence selection.
- Succinylcholine is inappropriate in denervation and many neuromuscular disorders because of hyperkalaemia risk.

**Monitoring and prevention:**

- Ensure an explicit sedation target before paralysis; monitor haemodynamics, oxygenation, gas exchange and ventilator synchrony.
- Train-of-four stimulation can help detect gross under- or over-blockade but results depend on site, oedema, temperature and electrode placement; fixed-dose strategies are acceptable in some ARDS protocols.
- Use quantitative adductor-pollicis monitoring for recovery when possible and confirm TOF ratio **≥0.9 before extubation** after general anaesthesia.
- Provide corneal protection, turning/pressure care, thromboprophylaxis, adequate nutrition and daily indication review.
- Paralysis masks both motor seizures and the clinical signs of conscious awareness, so consider EEG and sedation assessment when relevant.

**Harms and audit:**

- Persistent weakness, prolonged ventilation, inability to examine neurology, corneal injury and awareness under paralysis are key hazards.
- Critical illness myopathy/polyneuropathy is multifactorial (sepsis, inflammation, immobility, metabolic failure); neither all weakness nor every outcome benefit should be attributed to the NMBA itself.
- Evaluate an infusion by whether it achieved a measurable goal—better oxygenation, lung-protective ventilation or control of an otherwise unmanageable ICP trigger—and whether the least exposure was used.
- Record cessation, return of neuromuscular function and post-ICU rehabilitation.

## 10.11 Comparative perioperative assessment of the principal neuromuscular conditions

**Myasthenia gravis:**

- Assess bulbar involvement, cough, respiratory reserve, past crisis, thymoma and duration/dose of pyridostigmine or immunosuppressants.
- Relatively few functioning postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors cause unusual sensitivity to nondepolarising NMBAs; avoid unnecessary blockade or give carefully titrated rocuronium with quantitative monitoring and a sugammadex rescue plan, recognising that reversal is not a substitute for respiratory assessment.
- Continue pyridostigmine where possible, anticipate altered response to succinylcholine and distinguish myasthenic crisis (weakness from disease/insufficient treatment) from cholinergic toxicity (excess cholinergic effects), while acknowledging true cholinergic crisis is uncommon in contemporary care.
- IVIg/plasma exchange may be required preoperatively in unstable bulbar disease and for crisis.

**Lambert–Eaton syndrome:**

- Antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release.
- Proximal limb weakness and depressed reflexes can transiently improve with repeated contraction, and autonomic symptoms (dry mouth, erectile dysfunction) are common.
- Ask about associated small-cell lung cancer.
- Marked sensitivity to both depolarising and nondepolarising drugs and postoperative ventilatory failure risk warrant meticulous dosing, monitoring and specialist assessment; amifampridine is a disease-directed therapy.

**Myotonic dystrophy:**

- Myotonia is delayed relaxation after contraction, rather than ordinary weakness; cold, surgical stimulation, pain and electrical stimulation can trigger it.
- There may be conduction disease, cardiomyopathy, aspiration from dysphagia, respiratory weakness, sleep-disordered breathing and increased sensitivity to sedatives/opioids.
- Avoid suxamethonium because it may provoke sustained myotonic contraction and difficult ventilation; prevention of shivering, maintenance of normothermia, careful analgesia and postoperative respiratory monitoring matter.
- Myotonia itself is not reliably terminated by conventional neuromuscular blockade.

**Duchenne/Becker and other muscular dystrophies:**

- Look for cardiomyopathy, restrictive ventilation, ineffective cough, scoliosis and nutritional difficulty.
- Depolarising blockade can produce massive hyperkalaemia and arrest.
- Volatile exposure in dystrophinopathies may trigger anaesthesia-associated rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemic arrest, a phenomenon distinct from susceptibility to classic RYR1-mediated malignant hyperthermia; a non-triggering IV technique is often used.
- Nondepolarising responses may be prolonged and require quantitative monitoring.
- Check ECG/echo, respiratory function, steroid dependence and ICU capability based on severity.

**Multiple sclerosis:**

- Investigate relapse versus stable deficit, fatigue, autonomic and respiratory dysfunction, bladder infection and existing immunotherapy.
- Avoid hyperthermia because conduction through demyelinated axons deteriorates with small temperature rises (Uhthoff phenomenon).
- Neuraxial versus general anaesthesia should be individualised; neither is categorically contraindicated, and available observational evidence does not show that appropriate epidural anaesthesia invariably causes relapse.
- Long-term severe immobility increases suxamethonium-related hyperkalaemia concerns.

**Parkinson disease:**

- Maintain dopaminergic medication as close to the usual schedule as feasible; missed doses can cause severe rigidity, akinesia or a parkinsonism–hyperpyrexia syndrome.
- Avoid dopamine-antagonist antiemetics and antipsychotics such as metoclopramide, droperidol and prochlorperazine where practical; use suitable alternatives.
- Assess orthostatic hypotension, dysphagia, aspiration, delirium, cognitive impairment and deep-brain-stimulator management.
- **Cerebral palsy:** distinguish static central lesion from progressive musculoskeletal/reflux/respiratory complications; assess seizures, contractures, scoliosis, chronic aspiration, nutritional status, communication and access issues.
- These practical perioperative decisions matter more than disease labels alone.

items.title: 11. Disorders of consciousness, neurological determination of death and organ donation
items.priority: P2 HIGH (2 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (3 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 11.1 Coma, vegetative state and brain death are fundamentally different

- A patient with **coma** has no sustained wakefulness and no awareness; eyes remain closed, with no normal sleep–wake cycling.
- An **unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS)**, historically called the **persistent vegetative state**, describes wakefulness without demonstrable awareness: the patient has sleep–wake cycles and periods of eye opening, but no reproducible purposeful interaction with the environment.
- Diagnosis requires repeated structured observation after reversible confounders have been excluded, often with specialist neurorehabilitation input; behaviour such as visual fixation or command-following may identify a minimally conscious state instead.
- A **minimally conscious state** has reproducible but limited evidence of awareness, such as consistent visual pursuit, purposeful movement or intermittent command-following.
- The differential includes locked-in syndrome, which preserves awareness but severe motor paralysis prevents ordinary responses.

- **Brain death, or death determined by neurological criteria**, is different in both physiology and legal status: it is the permanent loss of all brain function consistent with the jurisdictional definition of death, established by a prescribed clinical process or neurological/perfusion investigation when testing is incomplete.
- In a patient declared dead, continued cardiac activity reflects mechanical ventilation, circulation and pharmacological support, not continuing consciousness.
- No ‘duration of vegetative state’ becomes brain death by definition.
- The historical curriculum terminology ‘brain stem death’ should be interpreted against current Australian/New Zealand requirements for **neurological determination of death**, not assumed to mean only absence of some brainstem reflexes.

### 11.1.1 Diagnosis and management of unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (SS_IC 1.78)

**Terminology and natural history:**

- The historical term persistent vegetative state maps to **unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS)**.
- It requires demonstrable wakefulness (eye opening and sleep–wake cycling) without reproducible evidence of awareness, and is distinct from coma, minimally conscious state (MCS), locked-in syndrome and neurological determination of death.
- The term **permanent vegetative state** is discouraged because later recovery is possible and prognosis is probabilistic; document the aetiology and elapsed time since injury (for example traumatic UWS four months after injury), rather than relying on a fixed label.

**Establish the diagnosis rather than inferring it from stillness:**

- Exclude sedative, antiepileptic or neuromuscular drug effects, severe sleep disturbance, seizures, systemic illness, hearing/visual deficits, aphasia and severe motor impairment.
- Repeated daytime and evening examinations may reveal fluctuating behaviour.
- The **Coma Recovery Scale–Revised (CRS-R)** offers a structured assessment of auditory, visual, motor, oromotor/verbal, communication and arousal domains; serial testing is preferred over one bedside impression.
- Reproducible visual pursuit, purposeful reaching or command-following should prompt reclassification toward MCS.
- In suspected locked-in syndrome, test vertical eye movements/blinking and preserve the possibility of intact cognition.

- **Investigations** support cause and prognosis rather than replace behavioural assessment.
- Review serial structural brain imaging (CT/MRI), EEG for seizures and background reactivity, and consider electrophysiology (including evoked potentials), functional imaging or specialist tests when results would alter counselling.
- Structural lesions, diffuse axonal injury and anoxic cortical/basal ganglia injury have different expected recovery trajectories.
- Neurological outcome cannot be inferred from the CT appearance alone.
- The 2018 AAN/ACRM/NIDILRR practice guidance emphasises that traumatic cause and MCS are associated with more favourable recovery than nontraumatic UWS, but individuals vary markedly.

- **Management** is active multidisciplinary care.
- Address airway, secretion clearance, dysphagia and safe nutrition; prevent contractures, DVT, pressure injury, pain, constipation, spasticity, urinary complications and recurrent infection.
- Provide positioning, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, sleep–wake structure, appropriate sensory stimulation and communication support.
- Assess pain despite limited behavioural expression; use validated observational approaches.
- Avoid oversedation where possible, because it hides potential recovery and impairs therapy.
- Where clinically appropriate, a **trial of amantadine 100–200 mg twice daily** for adults with traumatic UWS or MCS **4–16 weeks after injury** is recommended in the AAN practice guideline to hasten early functional recovery; renal function, seizure risk and local specialist practice affect prescribing.

**Prognosis, ethics and follow-up:**

- Use consistent repeated assessments, functional goals and neurorehabilitation expertise before high-stakes decisions.
- Separate treatment-limitation discussions from diagnosis of death; UWS patients are alive and have the usual protections regarding comfort, consent and care.
- Provide families with transparent uncertainty, review previous patient preferences and arrange structured review of complications and recovery.
- Avoid a self-fulfilling poor prognosis created by early withdrawal based on an unvalidated single examination.

## 11.2 Preconditions: exclude mimics before attempting testing

- The **ANZICS Statement on Death and Organ Donation (Edition 4.1, 2021)** is the central Australia/New Zealand reference and must be applied in the appropriate legal jurisdiction and hospital protocol.
- First demonstrate a recognised destructive brain pathology capable of causing permanent loss of all brain function.
- Then exclude confounders, including remaining effects of sedatives, analgesics, anaesthetic drugs, antiepileptic infusions, neuromuscular blockade, intoxication, extreme metabolic/endocrine disturbance and shock.
- Residual drug effect may persist for days after large infusions, organ failure or hypothermia; estimated five half-lives cannot be applied mechanically when pharmacokinetics are profoundly altered.
- If uncertainty remains, clinical testing cannot be relied upon as the sole method.

- The ANZICS minimum physiological preconditions include **core temperature ≥35°C**, adult **SBP ≥90 mmHg and MAP ≥60 mmHg** as guides, adequate oxygenation and absence of major endocrine/metabolic causes of reversible coma.
- Clinical testing requires a **minimum four-hour period** throughout which the patient is unresponsive (GCS 3), has nonreactive pupils, absent cough/tracheal reflex and no observed spontaneous breathing effort while ventilated.
- After hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy or prolonged hypothermia (<35°C for >6 h), wait **24 hours** before determination by clinical examination alone, unless appropriate evidence of absent perfusion permits a different pathway.
- These are Australasian standards; do not import United States testing intervals into ANZICS-based practice without checking.

## 11.3 The two independent clinical examinations

- Two appropriately qualified medical practitioners independently perform complete clinical examinations consistent with ANZICS and local legislation; one should be a specialist, with jurisdiction-specific requirements checked.
- The tests establish **(1) absent responsiveness, (2) absent brainstem reflexes and (3) absent breathing drive**.
- Each examiner performs the complete examination and an apnoea test independently rather than simply observing the other doctor’s findings.
- Examination normally includes:

- No response to noxious stimulus in the cranial nerve territory and no brain-mediated motor response to central/peripheral stimulation. Spinal reflex movements can persist and **do not** by themselves exclude neurological death.
- Pupils not responding to bright light; account for ocular trauma or pre-existing disease.
- Absent corneal reflexes; absent oculocephalic reflexes only where cervical-spine integrity permits, and absent vestibulo-ocular responses to appropriately performed cold caloric testing if ears/tympanic membranes allow it.
- Absent facial motor response to cranial noxious stimulation, absent gag/pharyngeal and cough/tracheal reflexes, and no other clinical indication of retained brainstem function.
- **Apnoea test last**, once all other test criteria and preconditions are met.

Avoid falsely interpreting ventilator autotriggering from cardiac oscillation or tubing movement as spontaneous respiratory effort. Conversely, a true respiratory effort means clinical testing cannot declare neurological death. Check spinal reflex patterns and device-related movements with an experienced examiner.

### Apnoea testing in ANZICS practice

- Preoxygenate with 100% oxygen; establish a baseline ABG, and maintain oxygenation without ventilatory assistance using the prescribed apnoeic oxygenation method (often CPAP circuit).
- Observe chest, abdomen and accessory muscles while PaCO₂ rises, and obtain repeat ABG.
- Under ANZICS 2021, a sufficient chemical stimulus is **arterial PaCO₂ >60 mmHg (8 kPa) with pH <7.30**, with a rise >20 mmHg above a known chronically elevated PaCO₂ baseline where relevant.
- In a stable patient this often takes approximately 8–10 minutes but is governed by gases and clinical tolerance, not the clock.
- Stop or adapt the test if severe hypoxia, haemodynamic instability or arrhythmia occurs.
- The ANZICS Statement specifically cautions against using an intratracheal oxygen catheter because of potential complications; follow its circuit guidance rather than substituting outdated protocols.
- In ECMO patients the sweep gas requires expert adjustment and specialist testing.

## 11.4 When a perfusion study is required

- Clinical testing may be impossible or unreliable because of major facial/ocular trauma, chronic hypercapnia with inability to establish an adequate stimulus, high cervical spinal cord injury confounding respiratory/cough responses, drugs that cannot be excluded, severe instability, or other limitations.
- Perform all feasible clinical examination components first, then request a study demonstrating **absence of cerebral perfusion**.
- ANZICS supports conventional three- or four-vessel angiography or radionuclide cerebral perfusion imaging, and permits CTA if specified radiological standards are met.
- It does **not** endorse routine reliance on MRI/MRA or transcranial Doppler for determination of death in its current statement.
- The imaging specialist interprets absence of flow, but responsibility for the death determination and its documentation remains with the appropriately qualified doctors.
- An abnormal or equivocal scan does not authorise declaration; discuss repeated assessment and specialist support.

## 11.5 Identifying possible donors without making assumptions about suitability

- Potential deceased organ donors include patients in ICU with catastrophic irreversible brain injury approaching neurological death, or patients for whom planned withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment may lead to circulatory death within a donation pathway.
- Recognition should trigger **early discussion with the designated organ donation specialist service**, not unilateral exclusion based on age, kidney impairment, infection, past malignancy or isolated haemodynamic instability: contemporary donor assessment is organ-specific and contextual.
- Eligibility depends on medical history, infectious serology, organ function, cancer risk, patient preferences, consent and transplant-service assessment.
- Some donors can provide kidneys or tissue despite unsuitability for other organs.

- Consent and death determination are separate clinical processes.
- The determination of death must be made **independently of organ procurement**; patients and families require clear, compassionate communication, culturally appropriate support and respect for prior wishes.
- In New Zealand, involve **Organ Donation New Zealand** and apply national legal and hospital procedures.
- The family should be offered an opportunity to understand and, if appropriate, observe the clinical examination; avoid technical language that implies the patient is ‘almost dead’ once death has been formally diagnosed.

## 11.6 Why donor physiology deteriorates after catastrophic brain injury

- Severe cerebral injury may produce an initial **catecholamine storm:** extreme hypertension, tachycardia and myocardial injury.
- Loss of autonomic control later causes vasodilatation, relative or absolute hypovolaemia and hypotension.
- Hypothalamic failure promotes hypothermia, central DI with profound water loss/hypernatraemia, and endocrine disturbance.
- Myocardial stunning, neurogenic pulmonary oedema, inflammation, coagulopathy, hyperglycaemia and infection may impair otherwise transplantable organs.
- Therefore, after death is determined, the donor still needs **active ICU care to preserve organs and honour the donation decision**.

- **Physiological donor support based on ANZICS Appendix F:**

| Domain | Practical care and why it matters |
|---|---|
| Monitoring | ECG, arterial line, core temperature, urinary catheter; serial ABGs, sodium, potassium, glucose, blood count, liver/kidney/coagulation tests; assess cardiac function where appropriate |
| Haemodynamics | Restore euvolaemia without excessive fluid; target adequate perfusion (ANZICS checklist suggests MAP ≈70–100 mmHg) with noradrenaline and/or vasopressin; assess stunning/cardiac output before adding inotropes |
| Temperature | Active warming to approximately 36–38°C; hypothermia worsens coagulopathy and arrhythmia and may impair graft function |
| Ventilation | Lung-protective tidal volume approximately 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, modest PEEP, recruitment/airway hygiene, target normocapnia and appropriate oxygenation (ANZICS checklist SpO₂ 92–97%) |
| Water and sodium | Detect DI by high-volume dilute urine and rising sodium; replace losses and use desmopressin or vasopressin as appropriate; prevent severe hypernatraemia and hypotension |
| Metabolic | Treat hyperglycaemia without hypoglycaemia; correct important electrolyte/acid–base abnormalities; assess nutrition and infection |
| Organ assessment | Cardiac echo/troponin and serial function, chest imaging/bronchoscopy in selected lung donation, cultures and specialist evaluation of organ suitability |

- Endocrine ‘hormone resuscitation’ packages are not equally established: vasopressin is useful for hypotension and DI, insulin for hyperglycaemia, corticosteroids may be considered in vasopressor-resistant instability or transplant protocols, and thyroid hormone is selectively used in some heart donor contexts rather than universally.
- Drug and procedural decisions should follow the donation coordinator and organ retrieval team.

## 11.7 Anaesthesia for organ retrieval after death and donation after circulatory death

- The donor who has been declared dead by neurological criteria does **not** require general anaesthesia to prevent awareness or pain.
- However, **spinal reflex movements** may occur with surgical stimulation and a sympathetic-like haemodynamic response can disrupt procurement; anaesthetists commonly administer neuromuscular blockade and sometimes volatile/other agents for physiological stability, with careful perfusion and ventilatory management.
- This is distinct from administering anaesthesia to a living patient.
- Protect surgical perfusion, prevent hypothermia and communicate closely with retrieving teams during aortic cross-clamp and organ flush.

- **Donation after circulatory determination of death (DCD)** is a separate process in which a decision to withdraw treatment is made independently based on the patient’s best interests and wishes, followed by observation of permanent circulatory cessation according to ANZICS and jurisdictional rules.
- The ANZICS statement describes **five minutes without arterial pulsatility**, confirmed clinically, as a key criterion in donation-related circulatory death determination.
- Withdrawal, end-of-life symptom management, death determination and procurement must remain professionally separated.
- The clinical team must never withhold comfort care to improve organ procurement.

## Case 1: A new fixed pupil during surgery

- A patient having evacuation of a traumatic subdural haematoma becomes hypertensive then bradycardic; one pupil is newly dilated.
- The dangerous diagnosis is acute intracranial hypertension with uncal herniation, though examine for pharmacological and mechanical causes.
- Announce a neurocritical emergency, confirm ventilation, oxygenation and MAP, check for venous obstruction, deepen anaesthesia as appropriate, and involve the neurosurgeon immediately.
- Give protocolised hyperosmolar rescue if appropriate, consider short-term ventilation to PaCO₂ ≈30–35 mmHg only as a bridge, and arrange urgent decompression or evacuation.
- Do not attempt to fix the Cushing hypertension with indiscriminate antihypertensives that destroy CPP.

## Case 2: Sudden hemiparesis on waking after cardiac surgery

- An intubated patient obeys commands on one side but not the other.
- Record E/V/M and pupils, check glucose, gases, electrolytes and quantitative TOF, and activate the stroke pathway.
- Bedside review does not exclude embolic large-vessel occlusion.
- Obtain noncontrast CT and CTA urgently, discuss thrombectomy candidacy, and review contraindications to IV thrombolysis in the context of recent major surgery and anticoagulation.
- Support brain perfusion, oxygenation, glucose and normocapnia; communicate the intraoperative haemodynamic and embolic history to the stroke team.
- Avoid equating a unilateral deficit with residual neuromuscular blockade.

## Case 3: Day seven after aneurysmal SAH—new weakness

- The aneurysm was secured by coiling on day one.
- The patient now becomes aphasic and weaker in one arm.
- Evaluate time course, GCS and pupils, review sedatives and sodium, exclude rebleed/hydrocephalus/seizures/haemodynamic collapse, and obtain CTA/CTP or other specialist imaging.
- DCI is plausible.
- Confirm enteral nimodipine, maintain euvolaemia and, with specialist agreement after exclusion of contraindications, titrate vasopressor-supported hypertension to neurological response.
- Consider endovascular rescue for refractory proximal vasospasm.
- Routine hypervolaemia or a universal triple-H protocol is not the answer.

## Case 4: Convulsions persist despite two small midazolam doses

- Five minutes of generalised convulsion is convulsive SE.
- Check whether the benzodiazepine doses were **adequate**; incomplete dosing is a common pitfall.
- Protect oxygenation, deliver a proper first-line dose without delay and load an evidence-based second-line drug at the recommended mg/kg dose.
- Perform urgent glucose/electrolyte testing and evaluate stroke, CNS infection, drug exposure and antiepileptic nonadherence.
- If refractory, intubate and establish continuous EEG with a titratable anaesthetic infusion.
- The priority is electrographic seizure cessation and cause treatment, not merely stopping motor activity.

## Case 5: Intubated GBS patient deteriorating after seeming stable

- On ICU day three, the patient has labile BP, reduced cough strength and rapidly worsening VC.
- These represent disease progression with autonomic involvement and impending ventilatory failure.
- Prepare experienced airway support before respiratory collapse; use serial mechanics, bulbar assessment and secretion handling rather than a fixed saturation threshold.
- Start IVIG or plasma exchange as directed, avoid succinylcholine, titrate alternative neuromuscular blocker only if required, and maintain cardiovascular monitoring for severe bradyarrhythmia.

## Case 6: Intubated patient with severe brain injury and no response

- An absent movement response after 48 hours of high-dose sedative infusion does not establish brain death.
- Review drug exposure, organ clearance, temperature, neuromuscular blockade, metabolic and endocrine disturbances and evidence for destructive brain pathology.
- In ANZICS practice, establish the specific physiological preconditions, appropriate observation period, two independent clinical examinations and apnoea testing with documented PaCO₂/pH criteria, or a perfusion study when testing cannot be completed.
- If death is determined, explain carefully to family and separately consider donor referral.
- Maintain physiological support to preserve organs where donation is appropriate.

## Case 7: Post-pituitary surgery urine output 800 mL/h

- Check serum sodium and glucose, osmolality, urine osmolality/specific gravity, haemodynamics and recent mannitol/diuretic exposure.
- If the urine is dilute and serum sodium is rising, central DI is likely.
- Replace water and circulation deficits, prescribe carefully titrated desmopressin with hourly urine output and frequent serum sodium monitoring, and anticipate a delayed SIADH phase after pituitary surgery.
- Conversely, a SAH patient who is hyponatraemic, polyuric and hypovolaemic may have CSW and requires sodium/volume replacement rather than water restriction.

## Case 8: Chronic spinal cord injury with abrupt severe hypertension in theatre

- A patient with chronic T4 injury develops BP 220/120 and bradycardia during urinary instrumentation.
- Think autonomic dysreflexia.
- Stop stimulation, check catheter obstruction and bladder distension, ensure adequate anaesthetic block/analgesia, sit up if clinically possible and give a controlled short-acting antihypertensive if dangerous hypertension persists.
- Rapidly removing the trigger can terminate the reflex; monitor carefully for subsequent hypotension and recurrence.

items.body:
- **1.** [DECRA, NEJM 2011](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1102077) — early bifrontal decompressive craniectomy reduced ICP but did not improve neurological functional outcome in the studied diffuse TBI population (Chapter 3).
- **2.** [RESCUEicp, NEJM 2016](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1605215) — refractory ICP decompression reduced mortality, with important shifts toward survival with disability; assess outcomes and values (Chapter 3).
- **3.** [CRASH, Lancet 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=CRASH+trial+corticosteroids+head+injury+2004) — excess mortality with high-dose corticosteroids after major head injury (Chapter 3).
- **4.** [CRASH-3, Lancet 2019](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736%2819%2932233-0) — early TXA in selected TBI, with benefit signal influenced by injury severity and timing (Chapter 3).
- **5.** [HEMOTION, NEJM 2024](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2404360) — liberal versus restrictive RBC transfusion in moderate/severe TBI: no established superiority for the primary unfavourable neurological outcome (Chapter 3).
- **6.** [SELECT2, NEJM 2023](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2214403) — EVT benefit in carefully selected large-core anterior ischaemic strokes, supporting broadened reperfusion eligibility (Chapter 4).
- **7.** [INTERACT3, Lancet 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10401723/) — coordinated BP, fever, glucose and anticoagulant reversal bundle improves ICH outcomes (Chapter 5).
- **8.** [ENRICH, NEJM 2024](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2308440) — early minimally invasive clot evacuation in selected spontaneous ICH; results not generalisable to every location (Chapter 5).
- **9.** [ESETT, NEJM 2019](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1905795) — comparable second-line success with levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate in benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive SE (Chapter 7).
