## Evidence audit and scope

### A1. Teaching coverage and boundaries

The workbook assigns **34 distinct parent LOs, 57 explicit components** to Set 6. The **27 ‘COMPLETE THIS SET’** outcomes are intended to be completed here; the remaining **seven ‘COMPONENT THIS SET’** entries are deliberately shared with other study sets and cannot be marked globally complete just because their neurological component is taught. The curriculum has been interpreted in the setting of current Australia/New Zealand guidelines and neurological terminology (for example, ‘brain stem death’ is taught through neurological determination of death; ‘persistent vegetative state’ is also explained as unresponsive wakefulness syndrome).

**Important allocation boundaries:** Set 6 teaches the neurological/muscular subset of BT_PO 1.5, the seizure/stroke subset of AT_RT 1.2, and the coma/ICP/status subset of IT_RT 1.2. It teaches the GBS, myasthenia and dystrophy/myotonia subset of SS_IC 1.88, **not** the separate tetanus/botulism components allocated elsewhere. For SS_IC 1.87, Set 6 covers postoperative neurosurgery, cerebral salt wasting and neurological deficits; the diabetes insipidus material is deliberately also explained here for safe differentiation but its formal workbook completion allocation remains with Set 5. For IT_PO 1.4, only cerebrovascular disease is covered here. For AT_RT 1.1, only raised ICP is covered here.

### A3. Focused evidence audit: what has been checked and why

**Ischaemic stroke (2026 AHA/ASA):** Current alteplase and tenecteplase dosing, IVT BP thresholds, updated EVT eligibility for large-core/basilar stroke, and harm from routine intensive post-EVT SBP lowering are incorporated in Chapter 4. **Haemorrhagic stroke (2022 AHA/ASA):** Careful ICH SBP 130–150 management in appropriate patients, avoid <130, reversal of anticoagulants, and differences in operative candidacy are taught in Chapter 5. **Aneurysmal SAH (2023 AHA/ASA):** Nimodipine, euvolaemia rather than prophylactic hypervolaemia, avoidance of routine statins/IV magnesium and multimodal DCI diagnosis are in Chapter 6. **TBI (Brain Trauma Foundation; 2026 BJA Education):** ICP >22, CPP 60–70, secondary insult prevention, decompressive surgery evidence and multimodal uncertainties are taught in Chapter 3. **Spinal cord injury (2024 guideline):** Weak-evidence MAP augmentation 75–80 to 90–95 for 3–7 days, instead of older rigid targets, is in Chapter 8. **Status epilepticus (ENLS/ESETT):** Timed benzodiazepine and loading-antiseizure medication doses, EEG and ICU escalation are in Chapter 7. **Australasian brain death (ANZICS 2021):** Examination, minimum observation periods, apnoea test criteria, perfusion-study indications and donor support are in Chapter 11.

**BJA Education and Blue Book audit:** The October 2026 BJA Education update by Plummer, Jeffcote and Udy provides an up-to-date TBI reading anchor; the Daum et al. 2021 myasthenia and Hayakawa et al. 2022 cerebral palsy articles anchor the perioperative neuromuscular sections. Relevant 2025 BJA Education coverage of early ICU management of trauma and anaesthesia for aneurysm clipping has been identified. The 2025 **Australasian Anaesthesia (Blue Book)** chapter on post-craniotomy pain/scalp blocks informs Chapter 9; the 2023 Blue Book article Vasoconstrictors – friend or foe? provides context for intraoperative hypotension/perioperative stroke but its mechanistic speculation should not be treated as established proof. Other Blue Book editions were screened for topical relevance, but not every chapter of every past edition has been independently reviewed in full; that distinction matters for a truthful audit.

**Examiner-report check:** Accessible ANZCA final examination reports repeatedly test interpretation of SAH grading, the management of raised ICP/EVDs, status epilepticus, cerebral salt wasting versus SIADH, GBS/myasthenia, spinal cord injury, neurological deficit after anaesthesia/neuraxial techniques, and neurological determination of death. The 2024.1 report specifically assessed an ICP management/monitoring scenario and a myasthenia case; 2024.2 included raised ICP during scanning, polyuria in intracranial disease and impending brain death; the 2025.2 report addressed new neurological deficit after neuraxial analgesia, high thoracic cord injury and SAH intervention. These topics are integrated as ordinary teaching rather than copied as isolated questions.

**Limitations of the audit:** High-quality guidance may differ in special populations (children, pregnancy, ECMO, chronic hypercapnia, severe renal dysfunction and local drug availability). This manuscript is a comprehensive first-pass teaching resource rather than an independent prospective validation of every possible future exam stem. Trial subgroup effects and low-certainty recommendations have been identified as such; local guidelines and the clinical team remain authoritative for live patient management.

### A4. Independent depth-audit findings and revised coverage (6 November 2026)

This revised audit rechecked all **34 workbook Set 6 parent outcomes** against the actual teaching text, not merely the pre-existing location crosswalk. The 27 assigned complete outcomes all have a corresponding chapter; the seven component-only allocations cover their specified neurology subset and remain incomplete as whole curriculum parent outcomes by design. The original document had an important mismatch between claimed coverage and teaching depth for **SS_IC 1.78** (unresponsive wakefulness syndrome) and **SS_IC 1.7** (critical-illness muscle relaxants). Both have been substantially expanded in Chapters 10 and 11.

Other improvements are integrated in their clinical sections rather than appended as orphaned facts: postoperative cerebral versus spinal deficits (2.6), physiology-guided TBI monitoring (3.7), perioperative management after prior stroke (4.7), the September 2026 antithrombotic-ICH reversal update (5.5), EEG-based status epilepticus management (7.6), spinal cord syndromes and compression (8.7), postoperative neurosurgical complications (9.7), and disease-specific perioperative neuromuscular management (10.11).

**Scope and residual boundaries:** practical neurological examination, stroke scoring, cranial nerve examination and brain-death testing require supervised clinical performance and cannot be certified by a written resource. Advanced neuroanaesthesia for aneurysm clipping, vascular neurosurgery and other specialised techniques is deliberately assigned to Set 27. Tetanus and botulism are not in Set 6’s assigned subset of SS_IC 1.88. This is a source- and curriculum-mapped teaching audit, not a guarantee that every possible examiner stem or future guideline change has been covered.

## Primary guidelines and authoritative sources

- **1.** [ANZCA Anaesthesia Training Program Curriculum, v1.14 (December 2025)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-training/anaesthesia-training-program) — precise assigned components were extracted from the user-provided Set 6 workbook and crosschecked against the supplied ANZCA curriculum PDF.
- **2.** [AHA/ASA 2026 guideline for early management of acute ischaemic stroke](https://doi.org/10.1161/STR.0000000000000513) — reperfusion, BP management, EVT, glucose and antithrombotic care (Chapter 4).
- **3.** [AHA/ASA 2023 guideline for aneurysmal SAH](https://doi.org/10.1161/STR.0000000000000436) — nimodipine, DCI, euvolaemia, seizure and vascular intervention (Chapter 6).
- **4.** [AHA/ASA 2022 guideline for spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage](https://doi.org/10.1161/STR.0000000000000407) — BP, reversal, surgery and secondary prevention (Chapter 5).
- **5.** [Brain Trauma Foundation: Severe TBI, 4th edition](https://braintrauma.org/coma/guidelines/severe-tbi) — ICP, CPP and secondary injury avoidance (Chapters 1 and 3).
- **6.** [Kwon et al., 2024 clinical guideline for haemodynamic management of acute spinal cord injury](https://doi.org/10.1177/21925682231202348) — MAP augmentation 75–80 to 90–95 mmHg for 3–7 days (Chapter 8).
- **7.** [ANZICS Statement on Death and Organ Donation, edition 4.1 (2021)](https://www.anzics.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/ANZICS-Statement-on-Death-and-Organ-Donation.pdf) — Australasian death determination and donor support (Chapter 11).
- **8.** [Organ Donation New Zealand: donation after brain death](https://organdonation.govt.nz/icu/brain-death-icu/) — NZ-specific donor care context (Chapter 11).
- **9.** [Neurocritical Care Society ENLS: Status Epilepticus protocol](https://www.neurocriticalcare.org/Portals/0/ENLS%205.0/ENLS%206.0/Protocol%20V6_0%20Status%20Epilepticus.pdf) — emergency treatment algorithm (Chapter 7).

## BJA Education and Australasian Anaesthesia (Blue Book)

- **1.** [Plummer, Jeffcote and Udy. Update on the intensive care management of traumatic brain injury. BJA Education 2026;26:418–426](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.06.008) — recent TBI and monitoring review (Chapter 3).
- **2.** [Daum, Smelt and Ibrahim. Perioperative management of myasthenia gravis. BJA Education 2021;21:414–419](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.07.001) — myasthenia pharmacology, anaesthesia and crisis (Chapter 10).
- **3.** [Hayakawa, Pincott and Ali. Anaesthesia and cerebral palsy. BJA Education 2022;22:26–32](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.08.003) — CP physiology and perioperative care (Chapter 10).
- **4.** [Gordon, Naumann and Shilston. Early intensive care management of major trauma in adults: part 2. BJA Education 2025;25:115–121](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.08.005) — TBI/decompression and ICU priorities (Chapter 3).
- **5.** [Ng and Larkin. Anaesthesia for clipping of intracranial aneurysms. BJA Education 2025](https://libguides.anzca.edu.au/neuro/journals) — context for aneurysm surgery (Chapter 6).
- **6.** [Tan and Willington. Post-craniotomy pain: analgesia and scalp blocks. Australasian Anaesthesia (Blue Book) 2025](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1302) — appropriate scalp blocks, analgesia and safe neurological emergence (Chapter 9).
- **7.** [Australasian Anaesthesia: Blue Book editions, ANZCA official index](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29) — 2025 and earlier editions; includes 2023 discussion of vasoconstrictors and perioperative stroke.

## Additional 2026 guidance and sources

- **26.** [Neurocritical Care Society/SCCM 2026 focused guideline for antithrombotic-associated intracranial haemorrhage](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12028-026-02601-4) — 4F-PCC versus andexanet, platelet support and VHA (Chapter 5).
- **27.** [SCCM 2026 guidelines for neuromuscular blockade in adults with ARDS](https://doi.org/10.1097/CCM.0000000000007002) — conditional NMBA use in selected severe ARDS, usually no more than 48 hours (Chapter 10).
- **28.** [AAN/ACRM practice update for disorders of consciousness, 2018](https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0000000000005926) — CRS-R, prognostic counselling and amantadine for traumatic UWS/MCS (Chapter 11).
- **29.** [2024 ACC/AHA perioperative cardiovascular guideline](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001285) — timing of elective surgery after stroke/TIA (Chapter 4); [2026 updated version](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.06.017).
- **30.** [2024 consensus on symptomatic postoperative spinal epidural haematoma](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11456791/) — recognition, urgent MRI and decompression (Chapter 2).
- **31.** [ASA 2023 neuromuscular monitoring and antagonism guideline](https://doi.org/10.1097/ALN.0000000000004379) — quantitative adductor-pollicis TOF ratio ≥0.9 (Chapter 10).
- **32.** [AHA 2025 post-cardiac arrest care](https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/post-cardiac-arrest-care/) — multimodal neurological prognostication without premature conclusions (Chapter 11).

**Reading recommendation:** For Set 6, prioritise the 2026 BJA Education TBI update, 2026 AHA/ASA ischaemic stroke guideline, 2023 aneurysmal SAH guideline, ANZICS 2021 death/donation statement, 2021 BJA Education myasthenia article and 2025 Blue Book post-craniotomy pain chapter. Use the remaining references selectively as the chapter topic is studied, rather than reading all landmark trials before learning the clinical principles.
